full_text:
Three persons, including an 11-year-old boy, died and widespread damage was reported across Kottayam district as torrential rain that lashed the eastern high ranges from Friday evening triggered landslips, flash floods and overflowing rivers on Saturday.
Two of the deaths occurred at Payyanithottam in Poonjar Thekkekara, where a landslip buried a house in the early hours of Saturday. The victims were identified as Josephin Johny, 27, and his mother, Rejeena Johny, 49.
The landslip occurred when a section of the hillside adjoining their house collapsed following incessant rain, sending a large mass of earth crashing onto the building and burying it under debris.
Escaped unhurt
Josephin’s father, M.J. Johny, escaped unhurt as he was at a neighbouring house when the landslip struck. The couple’s two daughters, Jomit and Somit, were also away from home.
Josephin, who worked at the canteen of an engineering college at Choondacherry, had been recuperating at home after sustaining a leg injury in a motorcycle accident at Erattupetta about a month ago. Rejeena was an employee of a private school at Payyanithottam, while Johny works as a school bus driver.
Local residents said the landslip originated from the Idamala hillside, an area with no known history of major landslips. Personnel from the Fire and Rescue Services, the police and the Revenue department launched rescue operations immediately, but the woman and son could not be saved. Their bodies were later recovered from the debris.
Fell into pit
The third victim was Milan K. Shinu,11, of Thottakkad in Vakathanam panchayat. He died after falling into a waterlogged pit dug for Jal Jeevan Mission works around 10.40 a.m. Though he was rescued and rushed to hospital, his life could not be saved.
The heavy rain also caused substantial damage to livestock. At Theekoy, floodwaters rushing down from the hills inundated the dairy farm of Anil Kumar of Puthenpurackal in the early hours of Saturday, killing 11 cattle that had been tethered inside the cowshed.
Multiple landslips were reported from the eastern high ranges as the Meenachil river overflowed its banks, inundating low-lying areas. Floodwaters entered several commercial establishments in Erattupetta town, where traders said the flooding was worse than that witnessed during the devastating 2018 deluge. Shop owners estimated losses running into lakhs of rupees.
As the rain eased on Saturday morning, water levels began receding in the eastern high-range areas by evening. However, authorities warned that the runoff would raise water levels further downstream. By afternoon, floodwaters entered parts of Pala town as the Meenachil continued to flow in full spate after breaching its banks at several places.
The Manimala river was also in spate while its major tributary, the Pullakayar, witnessed a heavy inflow of water following minor landslips in the Koottickal and Kokkayar region in the Wagamon valley. Although floodwaters that submerged the Mundakayam causeway in the morning later receded, parts of Manimala town remained inundated, causing heavy losses to business establishments.
As many as 26 relief camps, including six in Kanjirappally taluk, were opened across the district, providing shelter to 567 people. Total 28 villages in Kottayam district were affected by the heavy rain.

full_text:
Several parts of Pathanamthitta district were hit by a flood-like emergency on Saturday after an unexpected spell of extremely heavy rain lashed the region from Friday evening, triggering flash floods, landslips and widespread inundation.
The district received intermittent rain through Friday before the downpour intensified overnight. Around 300 mm of rainfall was recorded in the Sabarimala forests, leading to a sharp rise in runoff and swelling rivers. The intense rain also triggered a series of landslips and soil slips in high-range areas, including Thannithodu. Vadasserikkara recorded 339 mm of rainfall in the 24 hours ending Saturday morning.
Ranni emerged as the worst-affected area, with the town virtually cut off after floodwaters submerged key approach roads, including the Ranni-Vadasserikkara road, bringing traffic to a standstill. The town remained under two to two-and-a-half feet of water through the day. Floodwaters surged into houses within minutes, forcing residents to move to upper floors, while many families remained stranded inside their homes.
Several families were also stranded at Ittiyappara, where rescue teams were yet to reach. A number of people took refuge on the upper floors of commercial buildings as floodwaters continued to rise.
As a precautionary measure, power supply was disconnected in Ranni and neighbouring areas.
Rescue operations
Rescue operations were led by teams from the Disaster Management Authority and the Fire and Rescue Services, which evacuated stranded residents using dinghies and coracles. The district administration also initiated steps to deploy additional rescue boats to the area.
The flooding caused extensive damage to businesses in Ranni town, with floodwaters entering most commercial establishments before traders could move their goods to safety. Shop owners estimated losses running into several crores of rupees.
The rapidly rising Pampa and Manimala rivers submerged several major roads across the district, severely disrupting connectivity. The Arayanjilimannu causeway across the Pampa went under water, while floodwaters also entered parts of Kozhencherry, Cherukolpuzha and Aranmula, prompting authorities to evacuate residents from low-lying areas.
Boating prohibited
In view of the flooding, the procession of Palliyodams (snake boats) scheduled in connection with the Aranmula Vallasadya ritual was cancelled, and boating on the river has been prohibited until further notice.
The Travancore Devaswom Board advised devotees planning to visit Sabarimala on August 2 and 3 for the Niraputhari festival to reconsider their pilgrimage in view of the prevailing weather conditions and security alert.
Water levels in the Achankovil and Kakkattar rivers also crossed the danger mark. The District Disaster Management Authority warned that the situation could deteriorate further if the rain continued and directed people living along riverbanks and in low-lying areas to move to relief camps without delay.
The authorities also prohibited travel to Gavi via Angamoozhi and along other high-range routes.
Despite the sharp rise in river levels, water storage in major reservoirs in the district remained within safe limits. Live storage in the Pamba reservoir stood at around 23%, while the Kakki-Anathodu reservoir was at around 39%.
Three relief camps were opened at Kozhencherry, Thiruvalla and Aranmula to accommodate displaced families.

full_text:
The Thiruvananthapuram City Cyber Crime Police arrested a Tamil Nadu native for allegedly operating fraudulent websites that impersonated the Kerala State Lotteries and cheated people by claiming to sell Kerala lottery tickets online.
The accused has been identified as Dinesh A., 25, of Pattukkottai in Thanjavur. According to the police, he created websites designed to resemble the official Kerala government lottery portal by using the Kerala Lotteries name, official logos and government address to mislead customers. The websites advertised that Kerala lottery tickets could be purchased online and promoted the service extensively through social media.
The police said the accused allegedly sent QR codes, UPI payment details and other digital payment options to prospective buyers through WhatsApp. Victims who transferred money were promised that lottery tickets would be dispatched to them by parcel.
Three websites
The investigation found that the accused had operated three websites, keralalotteryonlinebuy.com, keralalotteryonlinepurchase.com and keralalotteryonlinebooking.com, through which several people were allegedly duped. The fraud came to light after victims approached the State Lottery department, which subsequently lodged a complaint with the Thiruvananthapuram Cyber Crime Police.
The investigators traced the accused by analysing the WhatsApp numbers used in the operation, domain registration details of the websites and UPI payment information. The accused has been remanded to judicial custody.
District Police Chief (Thiruvananthapuram City) Arul R.B. Krishna warned the public that Kerala State Lottery tickets are not sold online through websites or social media platforms. He urged people to remain vigilant against such fraudulent offers and advised victims of online financial fraud or cybercrime to report complaints through the National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal (NCRP) or by calling the NCRP helpline number 1930.

full_text:
The lifting of trawling ban off the Kerala’s coast has failed to bring the much-anticipated cheer in the fishing sector as the shores remained inactive, thanks to inclement weather.
Though hundreds of trawlnet boats and workers, including migrant workers, had geared up to venture out into the deep sea for fishing after the 52-day break in the early hours of Saturday (August 1, 2026), most vessel operators had to postpone their plans following a warning from the India Meteorological department (IMD). The IMD had warned fishers against venturing out into the sea off Kerala, Karnataka, and Lakshadweep on Friday (July 31, 2026) and Saturday in view of possible gusty winds and inclement weather.
A section of boats went to the sea from harbours in Kochi despite the warning. However, a few of them returned soon as the weather was not favourable. A few large vessels, around 20 metres long, which proceeded to sail were yet to return.
“More boats will go to the sea in the coming days from Kalamukku harbour at Vypeen. In the initial days, we are expecting a good catch of pink perch,” P.P. Gireesh, secretary, Trawlnet Boat Owners Association, said.
The traditional fishing sector, meanwhile, remained disappointed as the trawling ban period did not help it much. Traditional and artisanal fishers expect the ban period to bring a bounty to them as only they are legally permitted to fish in nearshore waters while mechanised trawlers remain ashore.
“This time, the catch was visibly poor, mainly due to dry weather conditions. The lack of expected income has pushed the traditional fisherfolk into a financial crisis as it has affected their financial plans, including repaying loans availed to mend their boats,” Yesudas Parappilly, district secretary, Matsyathozhilali Union (CITU), said. He urged the government to conduct a detailed study into the traditional fisherfolk’s plight and announce a package for them.

full_text:
Beneath the churn of Kerala’s turbulent seas, two dead and five missing fishermen from Muthalapozhi, Vizhinjam, Tangasseri, and Neendakara bear testament to a stark human tragedy where survival at sea is pitted directly against survival at home. All incidents were reported during a brief window from July 29 while a blanket weather warning, banning all fishing operations, was in effect. For low-income crews, sitting out continuous days means total income loss, and abiding by warnings is a luxury they cannot afford. Meanwhile, officials confess that they are powerless to block unsafe departures at many centres.
Heightened risk at sea remains secondary to the immediate threat of starvation on land. “It is all about livelihood. Should we starve to death, or die at sea,” asks Andrew from Anchuthengu. Also, climate change is disrupting the age-old maritime knowledge traditional fishers have relied upon for generations. “We are long accustomed to reading daily wind currents and sea behaviours, but shifting climate systems now defy even deep-seated traditional wisdom,” adds Mr. Andrew.
Fisheries and administrative officials emphasise that comprehensive weather alerts and stay-at-home orders are issued promptly under the Disaster Management Act through , public announcements and messaging groups. However, authorities admit that physically enforcing these bans at every landing centre is virtually impossible due to limited manpower. Furthermore, officials highlight that venturing out during extreme weather leaves fishers beyond immediate rescue, as responding units would face equal peril in the hazardous seas.
“Fishing boats pay nominal premiums for government insurance, but ignoring weather alerts risks forfeiting coverage. We have provided compensation during prolonged periods of severe weather, but there is no systematic plan for lost fishing days, leaving financial aid entirely ad hoc during extreme atmospheric conditions,” says an official.
A meagre sum
Union leaders and activists argue that government stay-at-home mandates fail to address the core economic reality of fishing families, forcing workers to risk treacherous seas out of sheer desperation to escape debt and poverty. “By issuing daily alerts without offering guaranteed minimum wages or survival compensation, the State effectively strips fishers of their sole daily livelihood,” says Jackson Pollayil, president of the Kerala Swatantra Matsyathozhilali Federation. He points out that he relief provided in the past was a meagre sum, restricted to just one person per household, and delivered far too irregularly to keep families afloat. “When the department issues daily warnings telling fishers not to venture into the sea, they ignore the reality that these families depend entirely on daily fishing to survive,” he adds.

full_text:
In a series of changes for the National Eligibility cum Entrance Test (Postgraduate) scheduled for August 30, the Centre is set to expand the choice of test locations, give candidates more time to plan travel to their examination cities, and give them more time per question in the test.
The reforms are aimed at making the process more convenient for the candidates, according to the Union Health Ministry.
Union Health Minister J.P. Nadda on Saturday (August 1, 2026) reviewed the preparedness for NEET (PG) 2026 and directed all agencies to ensure the examination is conducted in a smooth, secure, transparent and technology-enabled manner. He assessed the readiness of National Board of Examinations in Medical Sciences (NBEMS), technology partners, and other stakeholders and stressed that every effort must be made to ensure a fair and candidate-friendly examination.
"The end-to-end question paper preparation and delivery process has been further reinforced through multiple layers of encryption, secure offline preparation, time-bound finalisation of the question paper shortly before the examination, and controlled digital decryption only at the scheduled commencement of the test," the Ministry said in a statement.
The NBEMS has also operationalised a dedicated email address for reporting impersonation, touting, and other unfair practices while issuing regular advisories to candidates to promote awareness and vigilance.
The Ministry said that to strengthen the integrity of the examination process, Aadhaar-based authentication has been introduced during both the application process and on the examination day. Iris-based biometric verification will be used wherever fingerprint authentication is unsuccessful, it said.
Under the revised system, candidates will indicate three State preferences for their examination centre, with their correspondence State being the mandatory first preference, enabling allotment of centres closer to their place of residence, the Ministry said.
Earlier, exam cities were allotted on a first come, first-served basis prompting candidates to rush to submit their applications as soon as the registration window opened, a source explained. Those who delayed often found all nearby centres filled, forcing them to travel to other States to appear for the exam.
In another key change, candidates will be informed of their allotted test city nearly three weeks before the examination, giving them more time to plan travel and accommodation, the Ministry said.
The NBEMS has also rationalised the examination pattern to 180 questions to be answered in 210 minutes, allowing candidates more time per question while retaining the overall duration of the test, it said.
The exam previously had 200 multiple choice questions with a maximum score of 800 marks.
The source said that recently, the exam had been conducted in two shifts due to emergencies or postponements but the 2026 edition will be held in a single shift to ensure uniformity in the difficulty level and assessment of candidates.
Earlier, candidates often faced stress as the final venue and location details were released very close to the test date, leaving minimal time to book travel or accommodation, the official added.
A total of 2,73,183 candidates have registered for NEET (PG) 2026, an increase of over 12.5% compared with last year. The examination will be conducted in a single shift across around 340 cities and more than 1,300 examination centres.
Comprehensive security arrangements have been put in place for the examination, including advance sealing and verification of examination centres, CCTV surveillance, biometric authentication, candidate frisking, deployment of signal jammers, dynamic comput, live monitoring through central and regional command centres, and real-time supervision by independent observers and appraisers.
More than 60,000 examination functionaries will be deployed to ensure the smooth conduct of the examination, the ministry said.

headline: Grey monsoon clouds hang low, almost touching the white domes and arched gateways of the Shiromani Shri Guru Ravidass Mandir.
cluster_text: Grey monsoon clouds hang low, almost touching the white domes and arched gateways of the Shiromani Shri Guru Ravidass Mandir. [SEP] Grey monsoon clouds hang low, almost touching the white domes and arched gateways of the Shiromani Shri Guru Ravidass Mandir.
full_text:
Grey monsoon clouds hang low, almost touching the white domes and arched gateways of the Shiromani Shri Guru Ravidass Mandir.
The religious complex, spread across 11.5 acres, marks the skyline along the Grand Trunk Road in Chak Hakim village, Phagwara, in Punjab’s Kapurthala district.
The Guru Ghar, as it is known among followers, is dedicated to the 15th-century saint-poet Guru Ravidass. It serves as a place of worship but has also become a symbol of the Dalit community’s rising economic, religious and political assertiveness, reflecting its gradual shift from historical marginalisation.
Punjab has an agrarian economy, with Jat Sikhs, the dominant landowning community, and Scheduled Castes (SCs) constituting a significant share of its population. According to the 2011 Census, SCs account for nearly 32% of Punjab’s population, the highest proportion among all States. Yet, historically, land ownership has remained concentrated among Jat Sikhs. Most SCs have traditionally worked as agricultural labourers for Jat Sikh landowners, the economically dominant community that has over the years exercised considerable influence over State politics.
For generations, the social hierarchy was reflected in religious and residential architecture, particularly in rural areas. While large gurdwaras were built by the dominant landowning Jat Sikhs at central locations, Dalit communities, historically landless and marginalised, often constructed smaller places of worship. Their homes, too, were typically located on the fringes of villages.
Today, complexes such as the one at Chak Hakim are changing that pattern. Davinder Kultham, president of the Shiromani Shri Guru Ravidass Mandir Prabandhak Committee, which manages the gurdwara’s affairs, says that small landholdings were among the factors that prompted people to migrate in search of better livelihoods. Over time, migration by members of the SC community to Dubai, the U.K., the U.S. and Canada played a significant role in improving the community’s socio-economic status, particularly in Punjab’s Doaba region.
Punjab is broadly divided into the Malwa, Doaba, and Majha regions, and the Dalit population is unevenly distributed across these regions. Its largest concentration is in Doaba, the region between the Beas and Sutlej rivers. Guru Ravidass was born near Varanasi into a Chamar family, a community traditionally engaged in leather work and historically regarded as “untouchable” within the Hindu caste hierarchy. After Independence, the community was accorded SC status as part of the country’s affirmative action policy in education and public employment.
On the land of a guru
“Today, the third and fourth generations of our community are living abroad. Money sent home by non-resident Indians (NRIs) has brought about a marked change in how Dalit families see themselves and what they aspire to,” says Kultham.
He says the Guru Ghar at Chak Hakim has largely taken shape thanks to contributions from NRIs, with nearly 70% of the funds coming from members of the Dalit community settled overseas. Although construction began in the 1960s, it gathered pace only after 2005.
“The land for this gurdwara was donated decades ago by a Dalit NRI who owned a textile factory in England. We run a school up to Class 10 for underprivileged children, where the fee is nominal,” Kultham says. The complex also has a charitable dispensary, a community kitchen and accommodation for travellers. “Years ago, this would have been unimaginable,” he says, pointing to a section of the complex where a sarovar (sacred pool) is under construction.
Chak Hakim holds deep religious significance for the Ravidassia community. Followers believe Guru Ravidass stayed here for about 70 days and held spiritual gatherings. Across the road from the Guru Ghar stands an older shrine, whose foundation was laid in 1845. Devotees believe it marks the exact spot where Guru Ravidass stayed. It was only in the 19th century that the ascetic Mahant Baba Hira Das, revered as a saint, identified the site as the place where the guru had stayed.
The power of money and mobilisation
Forty-five-year-old Gian Sheel from Dhaddey village near Phagwara traces his family’s story to his grandfather, who worked in the leather industry when it was still thriving in the Doaba region. As larger businesses entered the trade and local units began to decline, his grandfather migrated to England in 1952.
“My grandfather moved to England, where he worked as a factory labourer. Over the years, his earnings helped the family establish a financial footing back home. With that money, he bought around 26 acres of land in Narur village near Hoshiarpur,” says Sheel.
His grandfather also purchased a tractor, sowing and harvesting machinery, and livestock. While Sheel’s uncles and their children eventually settled abroad, his father stayed back to manage the family’s farm and household.
Sheel, who now runs a spice business and is a social activist associated with an informal organisation called Volunteer Indian Social Integration of Nationhood, says that while remittances from the NRI diaspora have contributed, albeit modestly, to the socio-economic empowerment of Dalits, government welfare programmes, both at the Centre and in the State, have largely failed to achieve the same objective.
“These initiatives fall into two categories. One comprises party-specific policies. The other consists of constitutional obligations, which must be fulfilled regardless of which party is in power. These include ensuring representation and implementing reservations in education, employment and politics,” he says.
In Punjab, he adds, the issue of promotions under the 85th Constitutional Amendment remains unresolved. Successive governments have also failed to create awareness among SCs about welfare schemes. “Genuine sincerity is lacking, regardless of which party comes to power.”
Sheel says the Dalit community has long been politically conscious in Punjab, particularly in the Doaba region. “The Ad Dharm movement, which sought dignity and a distinct identity for the “untouchable” castes, began in the Doaba region under Mangoo Ram Mugowalia in the 1920s. Around the same period, Dr. B.R. Ambedkar’s emergence in public life also contributed to the political mobilisation of Dalits,” he says.
However, he argues that divisions within the SC community have limited its political empowerment. According to him, the fragmentation of Dalit votes among the major political parties has prevented the community from emerging as a unified political force.
With the Punjab Assembly election due in early 2027, the Congress, the Shiromani Akali Dal (SAD), the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) and the Aam Aadmi Party (AAP) are all courting Dalit voters, underlining the community’s growing political significance. Leaders across party lines have been making frequent visits to various deras — socio-religious institutions that have long served as important centres of social and spiritual life, particularly for marginalised communities.
Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s visit to Dera Sachkhand Ballan in Ballan village, Jalandhar, on February 1 this year, to mark Guru Ravidass’s 649th birth anniversary, and his subsequent meeting with dera head Sant Niranjan Dass on July 17 are seen as part of the BJP’s outreach to Dalit voters. Leaders of the ruling AAP, the SAD and the Congress have also been visiting various deras to seek the blessings of their heads.
Poverty behind under-representation
Yash Barna, chairperson of the Guru Ravidass Tiger Force, an organisation that works on issues affecting the Dalit community, recalls how, in the past, hardworking members of the community were often denied fair wages in villages and towns.“During my childhood, I saw this in our village. They were either given basic daily meals by members of the Jat community in exchange for their labour or paid with a small share of the agricultural produce,” he says.
Barna says that while the Dalit community had intellectuals, poverty remained a major constraint. “As our people gained access to education and employment, those who went abroad also realised the importance of political and religious representation. Today, with the support of intellectuals, working professionals and the NRI diaspora, we feel politically and religiously stronger,” he says.
However, despite the community’s economic and political progress, Barna believes social barriers persist. “The Sri Guru Granth Sahib is installed at the Guru Ghar. Yet, the majority of those who visit are from our community. It is still seen as an SC space,” he says.
On July 25, members of the SC community gathered at Ambedkar Bhawan in Phagwara, which houses a gurdwara and a cultural and literary centre run by the Shri Guru Ravidass Sabha Trust. Most of those present were retired government employees living in the Urban Estate locality. Many have close relatives settled abroad, and a majority of the trust’s nearly 200 members also have children living overseas. Through the trust, they run a dispensary, a charitable laboratory and a computer centre for children. They see these initiatives as a way of giving back to society.
“Most of us are retired government employees. Our parents’ generation lived in nearby villages, and as our economic condition improved, we moved to the town. Many members of our older generation and many of our children and relatives have settled abroad. They help us financially in running these social initiatives,” says Ghanshyam, general secretary of the Sabha.
He says the trust’s expenditure broadly falls into two categories: recurring monthly expenses and infrastructure development. “These efforts have benefited not only the SC community but other marginalised sections of society as well.”
Sharing his experience, Parvinder Raju, who retired earlier this year as a senior manager at a public sector bank and now lives next to Ambedkar Bhawan, recalls how support from relatives abroad made a significant difference during his childhood. “My maternal uncle moved to England in 1977. My father worked in a government job and was particular about our education. There were five siblings, and all of us graduated. But those were difficult times. Whenever there was a need, whether for education or family weddings, my uncle would help us,” he says. Even during periods of illness, he adds, the family knew there was someone they could turn to for financial support.
Socially mobile
The impact of emigration is most visible in Jalandhar, Hoshiarpur, Kapurthala and Shaheed Bhagat Singh Nagar (Nawanshahr), the districts in the Doaba region, where an estimated one in three families has at least one member working abroad. Remittances from the Dalit diaspora have contributed to a marked change in the community’s self-image and aspirations.
Dr. Amanpreet Kaur, an Assistant Professor at Punjab Agricultural University, Ludhiana, who has extensively researched Dalit issues in Punjab, says international migration among Punjabi Dalits, particularly from the Doaba region, has played an important role in their social mobility.
“They have settled across the world and constitute a significant section of the Punjabi diaspora. They advocate achieved status rather than ascribed status. A large number are employed in the Gulf countries, and their remittances have significantly benefited their families,” she says.
In her 2019 study, Role of Dalit Diaspora in the Mobility of the Disadvantaged in Doaba Region of Punjab, Kaur argues that these developments have made the community more socially, politically and religiously assertive.
Varun Bangar, the sarpanch of Chak Hakim, where about 80% of the population belongs to the SC community, says the village has prospered over the years. “While the diaspora’s contribution to village development has been limited, remittances have significantly improved the living standards of individual families. The village’s overall development, however, has been driven largely by contributions from residents and government funding,” he says.
Pyare Lal, a former member of the Chak Hakim Block Samiti, agrees.
“At the personal and religious levels, the financial contribution of the SC diaspora has been significant. However, there is scope for greater support for village development,” he says.
Jaswinder Singh, a Phagwara-based social activist, says, “When marginalised communities build institutions of this scale, they send a clear message that their faith, history and identity deserve equal dignity and recognition. However, with a section of the community still disadvantaged, it is important that both the NRI diaspora and governments continue to support efforts to ensure they can live with dignity.”
Punjab Finance Minister Harpal Singh Cheema, who belongs to the SC community, says the State government is implementing several welfare measures for marginalised communities.
“For the first time, the Punjab Government has reserved posts for Scheduled Castes in the appointment of law officers,” he says. He also cites the Mukh Mantri Mawan Dhian Satkar Yojana launched this year, under which women aged 18 and above from the general category will receive ₹1,000 a month, while those belonging to the SC category will receive ₹1,500.
As Punjab prepares to mark Guru Ravidass’s 650th birth anniversary on February 20, 2027, the grand entrance gate at Chak Hakim stands as a symbol of the Dalit community’s growing religious, social and political assertion, and of its continuing quest for an equal place in Punjab’s social fabric.

A joint operation by the Army’s Intelligence units and the Rajasthan Police has uncovered a counterfeit military combat uniform racket in Rajasthan’s Sriganganagar district, leading to the seizure of nearly 1,000 metres of unauthorised Army-pattern combat cloth.
According to the Army, the operation was launched after a consignment of counterfeit combat cloth was seized in Bareilly in June this year. Investigators traced the material to a manufacturing source in Sriganganagar, prompting the Army’s Intelligence units to carry out a discreet probe.
The investigation identified a local firm as a key link in the supply chain, allegedly distributing counterfeit Army-pattern combat cloth to shops in Sriganganagar town as well as Lalgarh Jattan, Suratgarh, and other nearby markets.
Based on the Army’s interim investigation report shared with the Rajasthan Police in mid-July, a coordinated operation was carried out on July 30. Joint teams searched multiple shops across the district and seized around 1,000 metres of unauthorised new-pattern combat cloth.
Security risk
Officials said the unauthorised possession, sale or use of military-pattern combat cloth is a punishable offence and poses a significant security risk by potentially facilitating the impersonation of armed forces personnel.
The investigation is continuing to identify the manufacturers, suppliers, and distribution network behind the counterfeit military-pattern fabric.

full_text:
A new digital medical emergency referral system being rolled out in Rajasthan is set to transform patient care during the critical initial hours. The model will enable the tertiary hospitals to make preparations for attending to the patients even before they arrive.
Rajasthan is the first State in the country to implement the model, in which a referred patient’s medical history will reach the control room online before they arrive at the hospital. This will allow a team of medical experts to review the reports and stand ready for treatment.
Prepared and tested at Rabindranath Tagore Medical College in Udaipur, the Simplified Emergency Transfer and Urgent Referral (SETU) has already managed over 3,510 emergency cases across 15 districts in the State. The model is going to be a lifesaver for patients by eliminating the issue of “blind arrivals”.
Principal Medical and Health Secretary Gayatri Rathore said in Jaipur on Saturday (august 1, 2026) that the SETU would serve as a robust digital bridge connecting the primary health centres (PHC) and community health centres (CHC) in the remote rural areas with medical colleges and tertiary hospitals in the cities.
“The system operates using only smartphones, quick response (QR) codes, and a closed user group (CUG) network, eliminating the need for heavy investments in additional infrastructure,” Ms. Rathore said. As soon as a physician at a PHC refers a patient using the digital app, the complete digital data, estimated time of arrival and live GPS tracking will be sent to the tertiary hospital.
Before the patient reaches the hospital, the control room will alert super-specialists in the relevant departments, such as trauma, surgical, obstetrics and gynaecology, and paediatrics, via the CUG network and reserve intensive care unit or emergency beds.
Ms. Rathore said a fully prepared team of doctors would begin the life-saving treatment for the patient from “minute zero”, as soon as the ambulance doors open. Besides, every patient referred through SETU will receive a follow-up call from the control room on the following day to obtain feedback on treatment and hospital services.

full_text:
Encroachments, mostly houses and petty shops, were demolished by civic officials on Anna Salai in Gudiyatham town on Saturday to provide easy access to Government Taluk Hospital located on the stretch.
Officials of Gudiyatham municipality, which executed the work, said that most of the 120 encroachments on the stretch were built more than a decade ago. These structures are mostly extensions of existing shops and commercial establishments that resulted in reduced road space. “Such extension of buildings has affected traffic movement, especially ambulances, on the stretch. The drive was aimed at the safety of road users and to provide more road space for vehicles,” S. Dhanalakshmi, commissioner, Gudiyatham municipality, told The Hindu.
Municipal officials said that the drive was based on an order issued by the Madras High Court on a Public Interest Litigation (PIL) to restore the original width of the stretch by demolishing illegal structures on it.
Notices were served to those who occupied the stretch as per the court order. Affected families were also identified to provide them with alternate land of three cents. “Ambulances struggle to navigate the narrow space on the stretch due to encroachments. Pedestrians, including senior citizens and patients, have to risk themselves by using the stretch,” said T. Sudar, a resident.
Officials said that the demolition drive was also meant to restore the water channel on the route as most of the encroachments were built on it. The encroachments, mostly concrete structures, blocked free flow of excess rainwater during monsoon. It resulted in waterlogging in town.
The water channel helps discharge excess rainwater from storm water drains in town to Palar River. The stretch is two km, connecting key areas like Pernambut, Ambur, Pallikonda, and Katpadi with Chittoor in Andhra Pradesh. The stretch is also a lifeline for residents to go to bus terminus, hospitals, banks, market, and schools.
Demolition of encroachments has restored the original width of 40 feet. The encroachments had reduced the total carriageway to a width of 20 feet. Adequate safety measures like blinkers, reflectors, steel railings will be installed in the coming weeks. Speed breakers will also be built to prevent accidents, officials said.

He assured the audience that the government was working towards ensuring job security for the youth. “The chief minister has asked for some time to implement his policies,” he added.
R. He said students should not stop with their degrees but upskill themselves to get ready for the next stage of development of this technology.
Retired faculty members and staff were felicitated on the occasion.

[SEP] August marks the start of the countdown to the Northeast monsoon, the season that poses Chennai’s major annual challenge. Even as the city is dealing with the impact of a weak Southwest monsoon, the focus has shifted to ensuring Chennai is ready for the ensuing monsoon, presenting the new government with its first major monsoon test.
full_text:
August marks the start of the countdown to the Northeast monsoon, the season that poses Chennai’s major annual challenge. Even as the city is dealing with the impact of a weak Southwest monsoon, the focus has shifted to ensuring Chennai is ready for the ensuing monsoon, presenting the new government with its first major monsoon test.
The stakes are higher this year as meteorologists continue to monitor the evolving El Nino conditions. While the Northeast monsoon is known for its volatile nature, and often springs surprises, El Nino, a complex climate phenomenon that influences extreme weather, has added another layer of uncertainty this year. In its outlook for the second half of the Southwest monsoon, the India Meteorological Department has observed that the currently moderate El Nino conditions are expected to strengthen through the remaining part of the Southwest monsoon.
The outlook also presents a mixed picture on the global weather factors. While forecasts indicate that neutral Indian Ocean Dipole (IOD) conditions are likely to persist, some international forecasting centres suggest that a positive IOD may develop in September, raising expectations of countering the impact of El Nino.
Officials of the Regional Meteorological Centre note that El Nino is usually favourable for enhanced rainfall during Northeast monsoon. Recalling that 2015 was a strong El Nino year when Chennai experienced a deluge, officials say Northeast monsoon behaviour is shaped by a complex interplay of atmospheric and oceanic conditions and cannot be associated with a single weather phenomenon.
Given that the Northeast monsoon could still produce short, intense rainfall episodes, meteorologists underscore the need for robust flood preparedness alongside measures to safeguard water security. In response to the evolving climate scenario and growing concerns, the government has formed an expert advisory committee to monitor and assess the potential impact of a possible strong El Nino condition this year and recommend measures for preparedness and mitigation. The government on Friday (July 31) ordered allocation of ₹340 crore to augment drinking water sources across the State to ensure no shortage of drinking water in view of the rainfall deficit during this monsoon.
Prepared, but not fully ready
While the city appears to be partly prepared, a significant amount of work is still waiting to be completed before the onset of the Northeast monsoon. A major concern among the residents is whether the remaining stormwater drain work, missing gaps in the drains, and canal improvement projects will be completed in time. For instance, residents of flood-prone areas of Velachery note that the civic agencies have informed them that pumps will be positioned at identified flood-prone locations and additional boats will be kept ready ahead of the Northeast monsoon. However, completion of long-pending flood mitigation projects remains crucial.
T.R. Subhash of Velachery says the 3.5-km macro drain from the Vijayanagar bus terminus to Thoraipakkam has not been desilted since its construction, despite being the area’s main stormwater carrier. While water hyacinth is being removed from Velachery Lake, a major groundwater recharge source, Geetha Ganesh, secretary of the AGS Colony Residents’ Welfare Association, says, “Velachery Lake should be desilted, wherever feasible, and made free of sewage before the Northeast monsoon. The focus should be on protecting the lake rather than on cosmetic beautification.”
The Greater Chennai Corporation (GCC) identified 87 locations prone to chronic inundation — based on the data from the 2024 monsoon — in its City Disaster Management Perspective Plan 2025. The report showed 26 high vulnerability and 27 medium vulnerability areas, while 34 locations were categorised as low vulnerability.
Councillors flag gaps
Elected representatives from some parts of the city, too, note that flood mitigation projects remain incomplete in their wards.
Puzhal’s Tamilaga Vettri Kazhagam councillor E. Settu says large parts of his ward still lack stormwater drain connectivity. Unless Puzhal Lake is cleared of encroachments in some portions near Surapet, the neighbouring area will remain vulnerable to flooding during the upcoming monsoon.
Some elected representatives have also alleged that they have not been invited to the government’s monsoon preparedness review meetings this year. Complaining that councillors were not informed of the decisions taken at the monsoon preparedness review meetings held at the Ripon Buildings, Communist Party of India (Marxist) councillor R. Jayaraman says that about 10 stormwater drain links remain incomplete in his ward in the Tiruvottiyur Zone because short-term tenders were not being sanctioned. The Corporation Council would pass more than 100 resolutions at this time of the year, including several related to monsoon preparedness. Only fewer than 30 resolutions were passed in each of the past two months. As ward development funds have not yet been released, councillors could not take up local projects, he says.
Mayor R. Priya has also alleged that the elected representatives had not been invited to the government’s monsoon preparedness review meetings this year. Such meetings enable elected representatives to raise constituency-level issues, particularly canal connectivity and flood mitigation requirements, she says.
Noting that monsoon preparedness work has started later than usual, she says canal desilting started a week ago. This year, tenders were issued only in July owing to funding constraints. No new civic projects are being cleared and even small projects and work on connecting the missing stormwater drain links are put on hold because of funding constraints and delays in administrative approval.
Mobilisation of volunteer groups for monsoon preparedness has not taken off either. Snehasri S., one of the two volunteers who submitted reports on monsoon preparedness following the flooding caused by Cyclone Michaung, says she has not heard if the GCC is re-engaging its volunteer network this Northeast monsoon. A senior official, however, clarifies that recruitment of volunteers will soon begin.
Every year, the Water Resources Department (WRD) launches comprehensive monsoon preparedness projects to desilt waterways and waterbodies in and around the city, ahead of the Northeast monsoon. With the government order for these projects being delayed, the department launched a special drive earlier this week to desilt some of the vulnerable sites with the support of non-governmental organisations and under corporate social responsibility initiatives.
This year, NGOs and citizen volunteers have been roped in. The drive has been extended to the catchments of key reservoirs, including Poondi and Red Hills. As many of the ambitious flood mitigation projects may not begin until early next year, the WRD is eyeing short projects, to be taken up with the State Disaster Mitigation Fund, to remove bottlenecks in the waterways and reduce flood risk.
Major projects under scrutiny
Concern has also been voiced over two ongoing projects — Chennai Port-Maduravoyal Elevated Corridor and Mamallan Reservoir — with environmentalists and residents pointing to increased flood risk, if adequate mitigation measures are not in place.
Councillors have demanded a study on the impact of the existing bridges and Metro Rail work on the Cooum’s carrying -capacity. Responding to the worries, GCC Commissioner G.S. Sameeran says the civic body has recognised the long-term importance of assessing the hydraulic impact of permanent structures on the Cooum riverbed. The WRD has entrusted Anna University with carrying out a scientific impact assessment of the piers constructed for the elevated corridor. The university will also recommend mitigation measures, he says.
While the WRD noted that it would coordinate with NHAI on the removal of work platforms during the monsoon, official sources in the NHAI say the elevated corridor design has been changed. The entire double decker structure stands on only one pillar. The NHAI monitored the water flow in the past two seasons, and there was no flooding due to the pillars. Work platforms are removed from October to January.
Similarly, environmental groups and fishing communities have alleged that the proposed Mamallan Reservoir, conceived as Chennai’s drinking water source, could increase flood risk in the low-lying coastal landscape between Old Mahabalipuram Road and East Coast Road. According to J. Prasanth, of Chennai Climate Action Group, converting this dynamic tidal landscape into a freshwater reservoir, enclosed by embankments and regulators, could obstruct the discharge of floodwaters during extreme rainfall, especially when heavy rain coincides with high tides or cyclonic storm surges.
Metrowater faces different challenge
This monsoon could present another set of challenges to Chennai Metrowater. The agency is strengthening water sources to sustain uninterrupted water supply until early next year, upgrading many sewage pumping stations and desilting sewer lines. However, the ongoing infrastructure projects to build new stormwater drains or gas pipelines often lead to recurring damage to sewer and water pipelines. In July, Metrowater received nearly 1,850 complaints, mostly pertaining to sewage block or overflow, following the collapse of ageing pipelines or the damage to the network.
Officials note that the issue continues despite sharing of maps of the agency’s underground infrastructure. They attribute the problem to the lack of coordination with other agencies when projects are executed. To address power outages during the monsoon, the Tamil Nadu Power Distribution Corporation Limited (TNPDCL) has instructed officials to prioritise buildings, including hospitals, public water supply and communication towers, for precautionary measures. Special teams have been formed for restoration.
TNPDCL Chairman and Managing Director V. Arun Roy has emphasised the need for speeding up maintenance work, including pruning of tree branches, to avoid snapping of overhead power lines and replacement of the damaged poles. TNPDCL has also identified sub-stations that got flooded in the past. A senior official says 18 sub-stations, including Perumbakkam, Manali, and Tondiarpet, were affected during Cyclone Michaung. Steps are being taken to prevent flooding.
Urban planning experts note that accelerated urbanisation, particularly near river basins, has intensified flood vulnerability by disrupting natural water retention areas. Anna University’s former professor of urban engineering K.P. Subramanian says that besides low-lying topography and inadequate stormwater drains, rapid but unplanned urbanisation is the pre-eminent cause of recurring floods in Chennai. Shrinking waterbodies have also led to flooding. “The government may consider making one of the secondary cities (Coimbatore, Madurai, and Tiruchi) as an administrative capital. Such a strategy may lead to the decentralisation of Chennai, making it less vulnerable to flooding and other natural disasters,” he says.
(With inputs from Aloysius Xavier Lopez, R. Aishwaryaa, R. Srikanth, Geetha Srimathi, and Deepa H. Ramakrishnan)

full_text:
The National Highways Authority of India (NHAI) has opened a ₹21-crore vehicular underpass on Chennai - Bengaluru Highway (NH 48) at Kadaneri village near Pallikonda toll plaza on Saturday for public use.
NHAI officials said the new underpass was the last identified black spot (accident-prone spots) on the stretch in Vellore. “The new underpass will help pedestrians, who are mostly dairy farmers, to cross the stretch safely. Ambulances can also use the underpass to help reach victims on time,” a NHAI official told The Hindu.
Of the total 13 black spots between Walajah toll gate in Ranipet and Krishnagiri, a distance of 148 km, five accident-prone spots are located in Vellore district. Of this, new underpasses were opened at Perumugai, Vettuvannan, Kinnimangalam, and Vallaram villages. The underpass at Kandaneri was the last facility to be opened. “LED lights, reflectors, signages, and blinkers should be installed on the new elevated corridor to ensure safety of motorists during night,” said B. Sampath, a motorist.
NHAI officials said that the new vehicular underpass below the elevated corridor is 5.5 metres in height and 20-metre-wide. The elevated corridor above the underpass is around 800-metre-long.
The new underpass can accommodate two-wheelers, cars and vans. The stretch has a few government schools, primary healthcare centres and car service centres.
At present, the stretch between Krishnagiri and Walajapet (Ranipet district), a distance of 148 km, has over 20 such underpasses, a NHAI official said.

full_text:
The verification of electronic voting machines (EVMs), control units, and voter verifiable paper audit trail (VVPAT) machines used in 14 polling stations in the Kolathur Assembly constituency continued for the fourth day on Saturday.
The exercise, which commenced on July 29 following the directions of the Election Commission (EC), covered the machines used in two polling stations on Saturday.
The verification was carried out at the electronic voting machine storage facility in Chintadripet, in the presence of Chennai District Election Officer and Greater Chennai Corporation Commissioner G.S. Sameeran.
The Electronic Voting Machine (EVM) Checking and Verification process being conducted for 14 polling stations in Kolathur Assembly constituency has so far found no evidence of malpractice, and should not be construed as a recounting exercise, Chennai District Election Officer G.S. Sameeran said on Saturday.
Addressing reporters after the fourth day of the verification process, Mr. Sameeran said the exercise was intended only to verify the reliability of the EVMs in accordance with the EC’s guidelines.
“This is not re-counting. This is EVM Checking and Verification process,” he said. “It is a 100% transparent exercise to establish the reliability of the EVMs.”
He said that in the eight EVMs verified over the past two days, the polled votes recorded candidate-wise matched the results in Form 20, while the preliminary mock poll had also been completed successfully.
During the detailed mock poll of one EVM from Polling Station 75 at Chennai Higher Secondary School in Kolathur, the VVPAT developed a technical fault after correctly recording 412 mock votes, with its indicator light failing to function.
Mr. Sameeran said the EC’s protocol permitted either replacing only the VVPAT and continuing the mock poll until the required 500 votes, or replacing the entire EVM set and restarting the exercise. However, the applicant’s representatives declined both options, following which the process was halted.
He said officials had also offered a randomly selected list of 10 EVM sets, from which the applicant could choose two for verification. “They were given one hour to select two EVMs. If they do not, we will randomly select two EVMs in the presence of other agents, videograph the entire process and complete the verification,” he said.
Responding to allegations regarding missing or incomplete seal markings on certain machines, Mr. Sameeran said, “All the machines have been properly sealed, and the seal identification is available. Their allegation is only that the seal is at the rear and not on the front. That can easily be verified by opening the machine and tallying it. In the subsequent stages, there are opportunities to verify and check the authenticity. They call it a technical issue. But that is not evidence of any malpractice or tampering with the EVM. We have explained all this to them in detail through a letter. Based on that, we have given them time.”
If they do not make a selection within that time, we will select two EVMs ourselves in accordance with the EC’s instructions and complete the procedure. The same procedure was followed in Kancheepuram by the District Election Officer and the District Collector, he said.
He added that if the applicant or chief agent chose not to participate, the EC’s guidelines authorised the District Election Officer to proceed with the verification through random selection, under videography and in the presence of officials, before submitting the report to the EC.
Additional District Election Officer and Joint Commissioner (Education) K. Karpagam, District Revenue Officer (Elections) N. Pushnadevi, and other election officials were present during the exercise.

full_text:
A book chronicling the life and legacy of S.N.N. Sankaralinga Iyer, the founder of Indo Commercial Bank and the India Cements, was released in the city on Saturday. The book traces his entrepreneurial journey, contributions to India’s banking and cement sectors, and it also highlights about his business principles.
The book was released by H.V. Hande, former Minister of Health, Government of Tamil Nadu, and Nalli Kuppuswami Chetti, Chairman of Nalli Silks, and the first copy was handed over to Gomathi Dhandapani, daughter of S.N.N. Sankaralinga Iyer.
Mr. Hande described Sankaralinga Iyer as a “polymath”, comparing him with great personalities such as Benjamin Franklin, for his ability to excel across diverse fields, rather than confining himself to a single profession. “He was farsighted and as a result he made forays into different fields,” he said.
Mr. Hande also urged the Union and Tamil Nadu government not to focus exclusively on attracting foreign direct investment (FDI) but to provide encouragement to domestic entrepreneurs who generate employment.
N. Kumar, grandson of Sankaralinga Iyer and Chairman, The Sanmar Group Corporate Board, notes: “For our family, thaatha (grandfather) was a deeply reassuring anchor. He was not emotionally expressive, yet he carried an unmistakable authority that stemmed entirely from his self-discipline and dignity. He commanded respect, whether he was discussing business expansion with associates or sitting on the floor with his grandchildren. His lifestyle effortlessly bridged the unyielding standards of a hard taskmaster with the profound simplicity of a devoted family man.”
Vijay Sankar, great-grandson of Sankaralinga Iyer and Chairman, The Sanmar Group, said: “The book was done to ensure that the man who laid the industrial foundation gets the recognition. He did it without seeking any applause.”
The project was co-ordinated and facilitated by S.B. Prabhakar Rao, a veteran of The Sanmar Group, who personally assisted Sankaralinga Iyer during the final years of his life.

full_text:
HYDERABAD
Minister for Irrigation and Civil Supplies N. Uttam Kumar Reddy has stated that every effort is being made to maximise utilisation of Godavari waters for the benefit of farmers in Telangana and reiterated that the government is committed for revival of the Kaleshwaram project barrages.
Mr. Reddy along with Ministers D. Sridhar Babu, G. Vivek and A. Laxman Kumar, legislators and senior officials visited Sriramsagar, Kaddam and Yellampally projects on Saturday.
Speaking after inspecting the three projects, which were getting the first significant inflows of the season. He stated that five pumps were switched on at Nandi Medaram pump house by drawing water from Yellampally reservoir with gravity to fill Mid Manair by using Flood Flow Canal.
“Our goal is to use every drop of Godavari water optimally,” Mr. Uttam Kumar Reddy said. He reviewed inflows, storage levels and pumping operations and insisted upon hourly monitoring and coordinated operation of projects to prevent any wastage of water.
The Minister strongly rejected claims that water pumped from Yellampally was “Kaleshwaram water”. He clarified that Sripada Yellampally was a Congress-era project conceived under the Pranahita Chevella project. The water currently entering Yellampally was natural Godavari flow and not lifted from the three Kaleshwaram barrages - Medigadda, Annaram and Sundilla, he said.
He highlighted that landmark projects like SRSP (foundation laid by Jawaharlal Nehru in 1963), Kaddam (1959), Nagarjunasagar, Srisailam and the Flood Flow Canal — all built during Congress regimes — continue to serve the State reliably. In contrast, he said Medigadda, Annaram and Sundilla barrages constructed between 2016 and 2019 under the previous BRS Government, developed serious structural issues by 2023.
Rehab on expert advice
The Minister asserted there was no political motive in keeping the barrages under free-flow condition and the government was strictly following National Dam Safety Authority (NDSA) and Central Water Commission (CWC) directives, which prohibit water storage until detailed investigations and repairs were completed.
A Central Technical Oversight Committee, constituted on June 30, was supervising the process. IIT Bombay and AFRY India were preparing the rehabilitation design and it was expected to be ready in 2–3 months. He explained that proposed measures include construction of a diaphragm wall and extension of the stilling basin to strengthen foundations.
Repairs would begin once designs were finalised, with efforts to restore the barrages before the next monsoon. Explaining why Kannepalli pumps were not being operated yet, the Minister said water lifted from there would need storage in Annaram and Sundilla first, both of which were under structural investigation.
He stated that experts had flagged serious defects in the secant pile foundation system, which deviated from the original Detailed Project Report.
The Minister accused BRS of running a misinformation campaign and trying to claim credit for water from the Congress-built Yellampally project. He pointed out that the previous government spent ₹1.81 lakh crore on irrigation but had created little new ayacut. Even Kaleshwaram failed to deliver stable irrigation to one-lakh acres, he alleged. Several other projects like Palamuru-Rangareddy and others remained incomplete, he said.

The vibrancy of Telugu language, culture and traditions came alive in Baltimore, Maryland, on Friday as thousands of Telugu people from across the United States gathered for the 19th American Telugu Association (ATA) conference, celebrating their shared heritage while strengthening ties with their roots.
The three-day convention is bringing together Telugu families settled in the U.S. along with their children born and raised in America, offering them an opportunity to reconnect with their cultural identity through traditional dance, music and authentic Telugu cuisine.
The conference was inaugurated in the presence of Maryland Lieutenant Governor Aruna Miller, a Telugu born in Hyderabad, lending a special connect to the celebrations.
A host of dignitaries from India attended the inaugural session, including Telangana Legislative Council Chairman Gutta Sukhender Reddy, Tourism Minister Jupally Krishna Rao, MLAs T. Rammohan Reddy, Yennem Srinivas Reddy and Manohar Reddy, besides Telangana BJP president N. Ramchander Rao.
The event also witnessed the presence of noted film personalities, including veteran actor Rajendra Prasad and playback singer Sunitha Upadrashta, who added glamour to the opening ceremony. Organisers said several more film personalities would participate in the remaining sessions of the conference.
Telangana Deputy Chief Minister Mallu Bhatti Vikramarka is scheduled to join the celebrations on Saturday.
Addressing the gathering, Mr. Sukhender Reddy lauded the Telugu diaspora for preserving their language and culture despite living abroad and for contributing to the development of both Telugu States.
The ATA also presented Lifetime Achievement Awards and other honours to distinguished individuals for their contributions in diverse fields, including community service, science and technology, performing arts, sports, medicine, entrepreneurship, business and journalism. Among the awardees was Ravikanth Reddy Ramasayam, who was honoured for excellence in journalism.
Other recipients included Kiran Chukkapalli, Sashi Gundala, Dr. Ravinder Regatte, Dr. Ramamohana Reddy Appannagari, Sudheer Rao, Raghunandan Nallanchakravarthula, Ashok Chintakunta, Madhavi Soleti, Akshara Devalua, Nitish Reddy Sudini, Sai Teja Reddy Mukkamalla, Esha Nagireddy, Dr. Ramya Chitrangada, Bala Reddy Indurthi, Dr. Vandana Devalapalli, Yennem Srinivas Reddy, Narsimha Reddy Koppula, Ram Matiapalli, Bhanu, Ram Annadi and Goutham Amarneni.
ATA president Jayanth Challa, national coordinator Sharath Vemula, co-coordinator Zeenath Kundar, convenor Sridhar Banala and several past presidents attended the inaugural session.
Speaking on the occasion, Mr. Sharath Vemula said ATA’s contribution to the Telugu community in the United States over the last 38 years had been unparalleled. He said the association had played a vital role in bringing together Telugu families while helping younger generations born in the U.S. reconnect with their language, culture and traditions.

West Bengal Chief Minister Suvendu Adhikari on Saturday (August 1, 2026) said eggs would be provided twice a week to schoolchildren through a separate arrangement while inaugurating an ISKCON community kitchen that will supply mid-day meals in Kolkata.
The kitchen, operated by the ISKCON Annamrita Foundation, is expected to extend its services to around 2.5 lakh students across nearly 1,800 schools under the Kolkata Municipal Corporation (KMC) within the next three months.
“Initially, ISKCON will serve mid-day meals to 44,000 students in 500 schools in Kolkata. Within the next three months, the coverage will be expanded to 2.5 lakh students. The allocation has also been increased to ₹10 per meal per student,” Mr. Adhikari said.

Taking a swipe at the Opposition on Saturday, Mr. Adhikari said it had criticised the initiative without first seeking clarification from the government.
“Without knowing anything, they started shouting ‘eggs, eggs’,” he said.
Opposition parties, however, have claimed that the government decided to retain eggs in the scheme only after facing public pressure and the possibility of protests.
Mr. Adhikari reiterated that ISKCON follows a tradition of serving pure vegetarian food and that the State government had no intention of asking the organisation to alter its practices.
“We will provide eggs separately. The Odisha government also follows this practice. I hope the Opposition will rest now,” he said.
The Chief Minister added that the government would take decisions based on the wishes of the people rather than the demands of the Opposition.
“We will do what the people ask us to do, not what the Opposition or the media tells us to do. We already have the blessings of the people with the support of 208 MLAs,” he said.

headline: 2,000 everyday artefacts, rare textiles go on display at Humayun Tomb

2,000 everyday artefacts, rare textiles go on display at Humayun Tomb
The collection, originally housed in the Sanskriti Kendra in Anandgram, was built by OP Jain, a 97-year-old Delhi-based paper merchant
Over 2,000 artefacts of everyday life and nearly 500 pieces of textile, including sarees, shawls and clothes used during prayer rituals — all between a century and 300 years old — will be made available for public view on August 1 at a new gallery that has opened in the Humayun Tomb Museum complex.
The Sanskriti Museum of Indian Textiles and Everyday Art is the result of a collaboration between the Indira Gandhi National Centre for the Arts (IGNCA) and the Aga Khan Trust for Culture (AKTC). The collection, which belonged to the Sanskriti Pratishthan, a public charitable trust, was donated to the IGNCA in 2023. The government-run cultural centre undertook preservation work on each of these pieces and textiles to make them display-ready.
At least 100 pieces of items like children’s toys, pots, jewellery, lamps, kitchen accessories, hookahs and chillums, beetle boxes, farming implements, writing equipment, mendicants’ objects and portable shrines made from a variety of material, including brass, coconut shell, copper, silver, ceramic and leather, are on display.
“This is who we used to be,” said Ratish Nanda, India CEO-AKTC, referring to the artistry of work on every single piece.
A child’s walker sourced from India, for instance, made in intricately carved wood, resembles a chariot, with a handle and three wheels. Another balancing toy from Rajasthan, also made in wood, has two male musicians on both sides of the scale, and a woman holding a sitar perched atop the central stand.
In the kitchen equipment display, all rolling sticks — made variously of metal like silver, as well as wood — have bells on either end, which point to an auditory experience that was part of daily food-making practices. Many of these items are no longer in use.
“These objects were not used by aristocrats or rich people, but were part of the everyday lives of commoners. We had so much beauty and artistry even in common objects found in the house,” Nanda added.
The collection, originally housed in the Sanskriti Kendra in Anandgram, was built by OP Jain, a 97-year-old Delhi-based paper merchant during the course of his peripatetic career. The Kendra allowed people a “sense of pride, and...a sense of being cultured,” Jain wrote in the foreword to a book, Everyday Art of India (1984). By 2023, the Kendra had one of the largest privately-owned collections in the country.
The new Sanskriti museum will also house over 500 pieces of textile, of which at least 90 have made it to the inaugural show. These include textile crafts like Kalamkari, Ikkat, Phulkari, Zardozi, Kashmiri embroidery, Jamdani among others.
The collection includes a rare pichwai of white cotton crochet likely made in East Germany in the 20th century. This particular piece depicts scenes of Radha’s ‘shringar’ (adornment) by gopikas, possibly to prepare her for the arrival of her beloved Krishna. They are bordered with cows, and on the outer frame by vases of plants with parrots perched upon the branches. “While the delicacy and exquisiteness of this work are truly outstanding, the object was framed and displayed at Sanskriti Kendra for more than three decades; consequently, it had deteriorated over time due to prolonged exposure to light, air pollutants, and fluctuations in the environment,” said IGNCA project coordinator and textile conservator Shakshi Gupta.
Gupta explained the effort it took by the conservation division to make such pieces display-ready. In this instance, it was first cleaned using a low-suction vacuum cleaner with a separator to collect its thick coat of dust. It was then put through nine washes, including two cycles that used conservation non-ionic detergent, which was then followed by four rinses to remove the detergent and dust while maintaining a pH of 5-6 to prevent damage. The cleaning result was measured using the whiteness index by colourimetry, followed by mechanical stabilisation of the loose threads stitched to the contrast new black lining, so the white pichwai pops on the black background. The whole process took two weeks, Gupta added.
The transfer of the collections from Sanskriti Kendra to the IGNCA is significant because “it is rare for private collections to go to the government,” Jain said. The collection was built to provide “joy and inspiration, to see how art was part of our every day,” he said. But it is tough to be a private collector, he added. “The foundation wanted to ensure that the collection stays for as long as it could,” Jain said.

Ajit Baraiya, a resident of Sunhara Mal village, died on July 27 while being transferred from Bamhani Hospital to Mandla with oxygen support
A 21-year-old died in Madhya Pradesh’s Mandla district allegedly after the oxygen supply in an ambulance cylinder ran out while he was being shifted to a district hospital, his father alleged.
Ajit Baraiya, a resident of Sunhara Mal village, died on July 27 while being transferred from Bamhani Hospital to Mandla with oxygen support. The administration has ordered an inquiry into the incident.
Mandla collector Rahul Namdev Dhote has constituted a four-member committee to probe the matter. “The committee has been instructed to submit its report at the earliest, based on which further action will be taken,” Dhote said.
Ajit’s father alleged that the cylinder ran out during the three-hour journey, leading to respiratory failure. The family also recorded a video showing the ambulance’s oxygen gauge at zero.
Collector Dhote said Ajit had been suffering from a severe kidney ailment for a long time. “He was referred to the district hospital with oxygen support. His father alleged that the cylinder ran out during the journey, causing his death,” Dhote said.
The opposition has raised the issue, demanding a high-level inquiry into the functioning of ambulance services in Madhya Pradesh. “There is a need to examine the working and facilities of the 108 services. This is a very serious matter, as a youth lost his life due to the negligence of ambulance attendants,” Congress MLA and former minister Jaivardhan Singh said.

3 dead in 10 days: Two terror attacks rock J&K despite high security alert
Two terror attacks rocked Jammu and Kashmir in 10 days. The first took place in Anantnag on July 22 and the other in Kulgam district on Saturday.
Two non-local labourers and one cop are among two victims of two terror attacks that took place in Jammu and Kashmir over a span of about 10 days. The first attack took place in Anantnag town last week, which led to the killing of Head Constable Aashiq Hussain Qureshi. That was the first terror attack in the valley since the Pahalgam killings in April 2025 that left 26 civilians dead.
The second terror attack took place in Jammu and Kashmir's Kulgam district on Saturday, leaving two non-local labourers from Chhattisgarh dead. While only one death was confirmed earlier, the injured migrant labourer later died during treatment.
More than one year ago, the Baisaran Valley witnessed a shocking terror attack on tourists, which left 26 people dead. The fresh terror attacks in a span of less than two weeks have renewed focus on the security situation in Jammu and Kashmir.
What is happening in J&K?
On July 22, Wednesday, cop Aashiq Hussian Qureshi was shot dead by terrorists at around 12.30 pm at Lal Chowk in Anantnag.
He was a head constable of the IR 3rd Battalion and a resident of Beerwah in Budgam district. At the time of the attack, Qureshi was deployed on Amarnath Yatra security duty.

Jammu and Kashmir chief minister Omar Abdullah and Lieutenant Governor Manoj Kumar Sinha condemned the “cowardly terror attack”.
"This heinous act will not go unpunished. J&K Police and our security forces are on the ground and will bring those responsible to justice," the Lieutenant Governor had said.
2 terror attacks in 10 days
Just as Jammu and Kashmir was recovering from the shock of the first terror attack since the Pahalgam killings, another such attack took place, this time in Kulgam.
Two migrant labourers from Chhattisgarh were killed as terrorists opened fire on them at a brick kiln in Kilam village, about 16 kms from Kulgam town. This was the second terror attack in south Kashmir in the last two weeks despite a high security alert.
One of the workers was critically injured and referred to Government Medical College, Anantnag, but died during treatment.

The last such case took place in February 2024, when two non-local workers from Punjab were shot dead by a terrorist in the Shaheed Gunj area of Srinagar.
The Pahalgam terror attack from April 2025 was one of the most brutal terrorist attacks India had ever seen. Hindu tourists were singled out and gunned down by Lashkar‑e‑Taiba terrorists in the Baisaran valley, and the incident left 26 people dead.

360-degree cameras, 8-member monitoring team: Ram temple trust starts videography of donations
Every stage of donation, from collection boxes inside the temple to the counting room, will be videographed, according to a senior Ram Temple trust official.
The Shri Ram Janmabhoomi Teerth Kshetra Trust has rolled out a new surveillance system to make donations at the Ram Temple more transparent and accountable even as investigation into the alleged embezzlement of devotees’ offerings continues.
From July 25, every stage of donation handling — from the collection boxes inside the temple to the counting room — is being videographed, according to a senior official of the Trust. An eight-member monitoring team has been deployed to oversee the process.
According to the senior official of the Trust, 360-degree cameras and SLR cameras are being used to document each step, ensuring a visual record is maintained from the moment a donation box is moved till the money is counted.
Officials said the objective is to bring in transparency, credibility and accountability at every level of the donation chain.
How the new process works
The Trust has also changed the way the temple’s 40-odd donation boxes are emptied. Earlier, multiple boxes were opened together. Now, they are being emptied on different days to allow closer scrutiny.
To manage this, two professional videographers have been appointed. Each exercise is carried out in the presence of two bank officials, two Trust representatives and two security personnel.
Once the box reaches the counting room, officials of the State Bank of India formally seal it after the counting.
The tighter monitoring comes weeks after an alleged theft of donations at the Ram temple triggered a Special Investigation Team (SIT) probe.
Police have arrested multiple accused in the case and the investigation is underway.
Also Read: ‘Attack on Hindu society’: Poonawalla slams Rahul Gandhi over Ram Temple theft skit in Parliament
The combination of videography, multi-agency presence, and bank involvement is aimed at removing any scope for manipulation and reinforcing public trust.
Officials said the new system will also help in quick audits and in addressing any complaints from devotees regarding the donation process.
Firm registered in name of accused's wife
The business operations and financial transactions of a firm registered in the name of Poonam Devi, the wife of key donation theft accused Ram Shankar ‘Tinnu’ Yadav, is being probed to trace any link with the alleged embezzlement.
Ashutosh Tiwari, the circle officer and the investigating officer, has written to the state tax department seeking complete details of the firm — Saundarya Construction and Suppliers.
Following a letter from the officer, the department concerned has begun collecting records.

70% water samples near abandoned Union Carbide factory in Bhopal found contaminated
Bhopal gas survivors’ groups claimed 70% of drinking water samples near the abandoned Union Carbide factory tested positive for faecal coliform contamination.
Around 70% of drinking water samples collected from localities around the abandoned Union Carbide factory in Bhopal tested positive for faecal coliform, indicating contamination, Bhopal gas survivors’ organisations said on Friday.
The organisations alleged that the situation is creating risks similar to those in Bhagirathpura in Indore after four groups of Bhopal gas survivors conducted tests following complaints from residents about receiving contaminated tap water.
Around 63 samples were tested from taps in 30 communities this month, and contamination was confirmed in 43 of them, Bhopal Gas Peedit Mahila Purush Sangharsh Morcha president Nawab Khan said, adding that 90% of samples from the Upper Lake supply and 25% from the Kolar dam supply were found contaminated.
“Residents living near the abandoned factory are suffering from diarrhea, vomiting, and typhoid,” he said.
In 2004, the Supreme Court had acknowledged groundwater contamination from hazardous waste dumped at the Union Carbide site and ordered piped drinking water to protect residents. “Now even that supply is contaminated,” said Rashida Bee, president of the Bhopal Gas Peedit Mahila Stationery Karmchari Sangh.
The organisations pointed out that in August 2018, the Supreme Court had directed the Bhopal Municipal Corporation to lay sewage lines and ensure proper drainage after complaints of faecal contamination. They alleged that the corporation had promised to complete the work in three months but had not acted in eight years.
Bhopal Group for Information and Action convener Rachna Dhingra demanded strict action against officials responsible. “There must be time-bound implementation of sewage and drainage plans and independent monitoring of drinking water quality,” she said.
After repeated attempts, BMC commissioner Sanskriti Jain could not be contacted for comment. Additional commissioner of the water works department, Tanmay Vashishth Sharma, declined to comment, stating he was on leave.
