NEW DELHI: The Dravida Munnetra Kazhagam (DMK) on Saturday moved the Supreme Court seeking directions to the Karnataka government to immediately release Cauvery water to Tamil Nadu, arguing that Karnataka must comply with the apex court's 2018 verdict and the recent directions issued by the Cauvery Water Management Authority (CWMA).The plea seeks an order directing Karnataka to implement the Cauvery Water Regulation Committee's recommendation, upheld by the CWMA on Thursday, to release 3,500 cusecs of water per day for 15 days to Tamil Nadu at the inter-state border point of Biligundlu."Direct the State of Karnataka / Respondent No. 1 to forthwith and fully implement the direction of the CWRC dated July 28, 2026, as affirmed by the CWMA on July 30, 2026, by ensuring a flow of 3,500 cusecs per day at Biligundlu for the period of 15 days commencing from date of the order passed by this Hon'ble Court, and to make good the shortfall in compliance from July 29, 2026 onwards," the DMK said in its plea.The party also sought a direction to Karnataka to clear the accumulated shortfall in water releases. It asked the court to direct the state to "make good the accumulated backlog of about 9.46 TMC due at Biligundlu as on July 26, 2026, computed on the pro-rata/distress-sharing basis, by ensuring releases such that about 7,000 cusecs per day is realised at Biligundlu over a period of 15 days".In addition, the DMK urged the Supreme Court to direct the CWMA to monitor reservoir releases in Karnataka and the flows realised at Biligundlu on a day-to-day basis and submit compliance reports.
The move comes amid renewed tensions between the two southern states over the sharing of Cauvery waters during the current monsoon season. On Thursday, the CWMA upheld the Cauvery Water Regulation Committee's recommendation that Karnataka release 3,500 cusecs of water daily for the next 15 days to Tamil Nadu.Responding to the growing protests in Karnataka, chief minister DK Shivakumar appealed on Saturday to organisations opposing the release of water to withdraw their proposed agitation. The farmer groups and pro-Kannada organisations staged demonstrations across the Cauvery basin, arguing that the state could not spare even a drop of water for Tamil Nadu because major reservoirs did not have enough water even for drinking.Shivakumar said the Kabini reservoir was rapidly filling up and warned that water could not be retained once the reservoir reached full capacity."Kabini reservoir is filling up. Once a dam is full, water has to be released. It is impossible to hold it back. I humbly appeal to those planning to agitate against the release of water to withdraw their decision," he said.Shivakumar also cautioned protesters against approaching water release points, saying, "Even if we decide not to release water, once the reservoir is full, it is impossible to hold it back. Protesters should not go near the points where water is being released. The force of the water can sweep you away. No one should lie down in the path of flowing water."The Karnataka CM said the state would protect the interests of its farmers while respecting judicial orders. "There is an order to release 177 TMC of water to Tamil Nadu, and the Supreme Court has upheld it. We must respect the court's order while also protecting the interests of our farmers. Our government is committed to safeguarding the welfare of Karnataka's farmers," he said.
He also accused the BJP of "politicising" the issue and said an all-party meeting would be held to consult former chief ministers, political leaders and legal experts before deciding the state's next course of action. According to Shivakumar, Tamil Nadu had sought 9,000 cusecs, but the Authority had directed Karnataka to release only 3,500 cusecs.The Cauvery Water Management Authority was constituted by the Centre in 2018 following the Supreme Court's final verdict on the decades-old Cauvery river water dispute among Tamil Nadu, Karnataka, Kerala and Puducherry. The Authority includes representatives of the riparian states as well as a nominee of the central government and is responsible for overseeing implementation of the court-mandated water-sharing arrangement.

NEW DELHI: Stepping up his campaign against the rollout of E20 fuel, AAP national convener Arvind Kejriwal Saturday announced a march to PMâs residence Tuesday to submit petitions against the ethanol-blended fuel programme, while demanding that consumers be given the option to choose betw-een pure petrol and E20 at fuel stations.Addressing AAPâs âNational Townhall Against E20â at Constitution Club, Kejriwal alleged Centre had âimposedâ ethanol-blended fuel on consumers without adequate consultation and claimed it was causing financial losses to vehicle owners. He said petitions would be collected Monday, before a delegation of about 100 people marches to PMâs residence the following day.Kejriwal placed three demands before Centre -- provide both pure petrol and E20 at fuel stations, price E20 lower than pure petrol, and reduce petrol prices to below Rs 84 per litre. He argued that consumers should be free to decide which fuel they wish to purchase.Claiming govt has repeatedly maintained E20 is safe for vehicles, Kejriwal challenged Centre to make public the scientific studies supporting the policy. âGovt keeps saying studies have found E20 does not damage vehicles. If such studies exist, they should place the reports in the public domain,â he said, adding that several people had shared experiences of reduced mileage and vehicle problems during the town hall.
He also alleged govt was only delaying the introduction of higher ethanol blends like E25 and E30 until the controversy surrounding E20 subsides. âThere are no studies going on. They are simply waiting for the issue to die down. Once it settles, they will bring E25, E30 and continue increasing the ethanol content,â Kejriwal claimed, advising consumers to opt for electric vehicles until E100-compatible vehicles become commercially available.At the town hall, several owners, mechanics, delivery workers and experts claimed E20 had affected vehicle performance, increased maintenance costs and reduced mileage. Among them was a couple who commute daily from Delhi to Gurgaon. The husband said their 2014 petrol car earlier delivered 14 km per litre but now gives about 9 km per litre, significantly increasing monthly fuel expenses. His wife, who works in the automobile sector, claimed dealerships were receiving complaints from owners of newly-purchased vehicles regarding mileage and performance, but employees had no clear answers to offer.
Motorcycle mechanic Aamir Khan, who has been repairing petrol vehicles for over a decade at Bhalswa Dairy, claimed he had witnessed a rise in complaints, particularly from owners of older BS-III and BS-IV vehicles. He advised owners to keep their fuel tanks relatively full to minimise air and moisture accumulation inside the tank.Dr Anupam Saini, an environmental scientist from DU, questioned the environmental benefits of ethanol, saying any assessment should account for fertiliser use, water consumption, land-use change and the overall carbon footprint of ethanol production rather than tailpipe emissions alone.

If someone from our side sports a body language of having 207 MLAs and hits the road, then the consequence will be disastrous," he said at event in Kolkata, referring to the number seats the BJP won in the assembly elections in April to form its first government in the state.âThe unwarranted egg therapy we see now can turn on its head and start falling on the other side as well. Everyone, including those in my party, must understand that. Those âSanatanisâ who have suddenly found a place in our party and are harbouring aspirations for influence and advantage must also remain careful because the trajectory of those eggs can change in no time,â the Rajya Sabha MP remarked, apparently referring to leaders who joined the BJP from the Trinamool Congress (TMC), which lost power in West Bengal after 15 years.The âegg therapyâ Bhattacharya mentioned alluded to incidents of egg-pelting targeting TMC leaders after the party's defeat.He also acknowledged that despite having assumed political power in West Bengal, the BJP has not yet been entirely successful in eradicating the "culture of extortion.""Our government has come to power only two months ago. We have not been able to solve all problems. If I say that we have been able to eradicate extortion from everywhere, then I will be making a false claim.
There are deviations. People had become accustomed to passing through a system of making easy money through syndicates. Not everything has changed with the change in state power," Bhattacharya told the audience."Some joined the ruling party (BJP) within four hours, others had dormant wishes that have now surfaced. We are trying to control such tendencies within the party. Our CM Suvendu Adhikari is also trying to apply strict brakes on such tendencies."Emphasising the need to free the business ecosystem from "partisan politics," the BJP leader argued that West Bengal stood at the "cusp of breaking with its chequered industrial past.""We must keep partisan politics out of this system. We have become residents of a political society in West Bengal. We need freedom from it. Till such time Bengal is able to come out of the culture of infiltration of politics in every sphere of life, no government can bring about its effective change and attract investment."
"We are making an earnest effort to build a government for West Bengal."Bhattacharya described the BJP's progress towards that goal as only a "partial success.""We haven't been able to provide you with an error-free atmosphere, but we have largely been able to deliver an investment climate that is fear-free. To set up a company, you can now buy your own brick, cement and sand. If someone approaches you, use the phone. He will either leave your premises or find himself inside a lock-up."(With PTI inputs)

Anti-paper leak law gets President's nod (Representative image)
NEW DELHI: The Centre's tougher anti-paper leak law has officially come into force from Saturday after President Droupadi Murmu gave her assent to the Public Examinations (Prevention of Unfair Means) Amendment Bill, 2026, paving the way for stricter punishment, time-bound investigations and fast-track trials in public examination fraud cases.The amended law, which was passed by both Houses of Parliament earlier this week, is aimed at cracking down on paper leaks and organised examination fraud following nationwide protests over the NEET-2026 paper leak.The legislation strengthens the Public Examinations (Prevention of Unfair Means) Act, 2024, which was enacted after a series of examination paper leak controversies but is now being expanded with tougher provisions.
What changes from today?
With the law now in force, several key changes will take immediate effect:
Time-bound investigation and trial
One of the biggest changes is that investigations into paper leak cases must now be completed within two months.After a chargesheet is filed, states and Union Territories will be required to set up fast-track courts, which must complete trials within three months.The aim is to ensure quicker disposal of cases that often remained pending for years.
Harsher punishment
The amended law significantly increases the punishment for those involved in examination fraud.Individuals found guilty of paper leaks or using unfair means in public examinations will face:
Minimum imprisonment of five years
Maximum imprisonment of 10 years
Fine of up to Rs 50 lakh
For organised examination fraud or paper leak rackets, the punishment is even stricter:
Minimum imprisonment of seven years
Fine of up to Rs 10 crore
The amendments enhance penalties prescribed under the 2024 law.
What acts are now punishable?
The legislation identifies 15 offences related to public examinations.These include:
Leaking question papers
Tampering with OMR sheets
Creating fake examination websites
Issuing fake admit cards
Other organised methods used to manipulate public examinations
The law is intended to target both individuals and organised criminal networks involved in examination fraud.
Which exams are covered?
Like the 2024 Act, the amended law applies to public examinations conducted by the Central government and its agencies, including:
Union Public Service Commission (UPSC)
Staff Selection Commission (SSC)
National Testing Agency (NTA)
Railway recruitment examinations
Banking recruitment examinations
Other notified central public examinations
Before the 2024 legislation, there was no dedicated substantive law dealing specifically with unfair means adopted in central public examinations.
Why was the law amended?
The amendments come after widespread protests over the NEET-2026 paper leak, which triggered demonstrations in Delhi and several other parts of the country.The government accelerated passage of the Bill after Prime Minister Narendra Modi promised stronger legal safeguards and fast-track courts to deal with examination fraud.Parliament cleared the Bill this week with provisions for enhanced punishment, special courts and faster investigations.During the debate, Union minister Jitendra Singh said the government remained committed to a "zero tolerance" approach towards paper leaks and was open to strengthening the law following recent events.Following Parliament's approval of the Bill, Prime Minister Narendra Modi described it as "an important step towards building a credible exam system" and said the government would not spare those responsible for paper leaks.In a selfie-video message, he said gangs involved in leaking examination papers were "playing with the future of students" and stressed that stringent laws were necessary to tackle the menace.
PM Modi noted that paper leaks had affected both states and the Centre for decades, making reforms in the examination system essential. He also said the government had taken several steps, including constituting a task force, setting up fast-track courts and promoting greater use of technology, while reaffirming its "zero tolerance" approach towards examination fraud.
Aim of the amended law
The Centre says the amended legislation is designed to create a stronger legal framework against examination fraud by ensuring:
Faster investigations
Speedy trials through fast-track courts
Stricter punishment for offenders
Greater deterrence against organised paper leak networks
The law forms part of the government's broader effort to strengthen the integrity of public examinations following repeated incidents of question paper leaks across the country.

KULGAM: Panic. Shuttered doors. Phones ringing with anxious calls from home. Brick kilns across south Kashmir ground to a halt Saturday as migrant labourers stayed indoors, rattled by the killing of two co-workers barely 2km away and wondering if they should leave â or stay and earn.Around 11am, Sunil Kumar, 34, and fellow labourer Renku Yadav stepped out of brick kiln No 515 in Hablishi village of Kulgam district to buy atta and pulses after running out of food. They had barely walked a short distance when the kiln owner chased after them, urging them to return.Fear had settled over the village after terrorists fatally shot two migrant labourers Friday evening at a brick kiln in neighbouring Kilam â killing Deepak Ratrey, 24, and Bhupendra Bhaina, 28, from Chhattisgarh.The attack raised concerns about the resurgence of targeted killings of non-native people in Kashmir. In 2022, a series of targeted attacks resulted in the deaths of at least 10 labourers.Terrorists tend to target âsoft targetsâ such as migrant workers, who arrive in Kashmir every year between March and Nov â the seasonal workforce engaged in labour-intensive tasks on farms, construction sites and brick kilns.Kumar lives beside the kiln in a shelter built by stacking bricks without cement.
The temporary rooms become home during the brick-making season.He has worked in J&K since 2007 and has spent nearly a decade at the same kiln, moulding clay bricks before they are fired. âLife has been peaceful in recent years. We work during the day, cook in the evening, listen to songs and speak to our families,â Kumar said.âWe have seen such attacks in Kashmir, but what can a labourer do? We have to earn a living,â said Kumar, who came from Lucknow on July 16 with 12 more men for a monthly wage of Rs 18,000.Brick kiln owners fear a repeat of earlier years when attacks on migrant workers triggered an exodus, crippling businesses dependent on seasonal labour. âWe came here for three months. We donât think the situation is so bad that we should leave immediately,â Kumar assured.
Zakir Ansari, 23, from Bareilly said he and nine men reached Kashmir in early July through a contractor. âOur family called all night worried, but we told them we were fine,â he said, adding that security personnel visited and assured their safety.Lt governor Manoj Sinha chaired a security review and directed officials to protect migrant workers. CM Omar Abdullah condemned the killings and announced Rs 10 lakh each for the victimsâ families, in addition to Rs 6 lakh being provided by district administration.Political ripples followed the killings. NC president Dr Farooq Abdullah questioned why such attacks surface whenever the demand for restoration of J&Kâs statehood gathers momentum, drawing sharp criticism from BJP and PDP. BJPâs Sunil Sharma called the remarks âvery strangeâ, while PDP functionary Iltija Mufti urged that âa moment of grief shouldnât be politicisedâ.

The attack took place late Friday night in the Kelam area of south Kashmir (File photo)
NEW DELHI: The death toll in Friday night's terror attack on migrant labourers in Jammu and Kashmir's Kulgam rose to two on Saturday after a Chhattisgarh worker succumbed to injuries in hospital, officials told news agency PTI.The attack took place late Friday night in the Kelam area of south Kashmir, where the two workers were employed at a brick kiln. Officials said both men sustained critical injuries after terrorists fired at them.
One of the labourers, identified as Deepak Ratray, died before he could be shifted to a hospital. The second victim, Bopinder, was initially admitted to Government Medical College (GMC) Anantnag before being referred to SKIMS Hospital in Soura, where he later succumbed to his injuries.Officials said both victims were in their twenties and had travelled from Chhattisgarh in search of work.The incident comes days after terrorists shot dead Jammu and Kashmir Police head constable Ashiq Hussain Qureshi at Anantnag's Lal Chowk while he was deployed on Amarnath Yatra duty. That attack, on July 22, was the first terror strike in Kashmir since the April 22, 2025 Pahalgam massacre, in which 26 people were killed.
Friday's attack has also revived concerns over the safety of migrant workers in the Valley. In February 2024, two non-local labourers from Punjab, Amritpal Singh and Rohit Masih, were shot dead in Srinagar. Before that, in October 2021, terrorists killed two workers from Bihar, Raja Reshi Dev and Joginder Reshi Dev, in Kulgam's Wanpoh area.Lieutenant governor Manoj Sinha condemned the latest attack and said security forces had been instructed to intensify anti-terror operations."I strongly condemn this cowardly act. I have directed our security forces to step up their operations and eliminate the terrorists," Sinha wrote on X, adding that he had spoken to DGP Nalin Prabhat and other senior security officials.PDP president and former chief minister Mehbooba Mufti also condemned the killings.
"They work themselves to the bone far away from home only to feed their families. Unimaginably cruel to target them in such senseless acts of violence," she said.BJP's Jammu and Kashmir spokesperson Altaf Thakur described the attack as "cowardly, barbaric and inhuman", alleging that its objective was to disturb peace and normalcy in the Union Territory.The attack occurred during the ongoing Amarnath Yatra, which began on July 3. While the pilgrimage through the Pahalgam route has remained suspended since July 19 because of heavy rain and landslides, the Baltal route in Ganderbal continues to remain operational.Following the attack, security forces launched a cordon-and-search operation in the area to trace those responsible.

Rahul Gandhi took a jab at PM Modi and Amit Shah, calling them 'India's past'
NEW DELHI: Leader of Opposition in the Lok Sabha Rahul Gandhi on Friday targeted Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Union Home Minister Amit Shah over the action against student protesters, alleging that the government was trying to "silence Gen Z" through FIRs and social media takedowns after directly attacking them during protests.Making a statement on X, the Congress leader said, "PM Modi and Amit Shah - you cannot threaten Gen Z into silence. First you broke their bones. Now you are filing FIRs and taking down their accounts."
Further taking a jab at PM Modi and Shah, he added, "You are Indiaâs past. Be careful about how you treat Indiaâs future."
This comes a day after Rahul demanded a Supreme Court-monitored, high-powered committee to investigate the alleged police action against student protesters during the July 20 demonstration at Delhi's Jantar Mantar.In a post on X, the Congress MP had called for an impartial probe into the alleged use of force, saying, "Students deserve justice. An independent SC-monitored high-powered committee must be constituted to probe brutalities against our students."
Gandhi also shared a video purportedly showing police action against the protesters. The footage appeared to show police personnel lathi-charging demonstrators, while another clip showed a man in civilian clothes forcefully pushing a student carrying the Indian flag onto the road.
His demand came as Opposition MPs from several INDIA bloc parties staged a protest at Makar Dwar in the Parliament complex over the alleged police action against students and the alleged embezzlement of donations meant for the Ram Temple in Ayodhya.The MPs gathered around 10.30 am, carrying placards questioning who ordered the police action at Jantar Mantar and raising slogans demanding accountability from the Centre over the alleged use of force and the alleged financial irregularities in donations to the Shri Ram Janmabhoomi Temple.
The protest took place hours before the Rajya Sabha was scheduled to consider and pass the Public Examinations (Prevention of Unfair Means) Amendment Bill, 2026.

NEW DELHI: The Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI) has launched a fresh enforcement drive against food business operators, issuing a product recall, suspending a manufacturing licence and prohibiting the sale of a health supplement over serious violations of food safety regulations.In one action, FSSAI ordered M/s Sun Organic Industries Pvt Ltd to immediately recall its Wonderland Raisins after regulatory testing found pesticide residues exceeding the prescribed limits. It warned that violations of the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006, would invite strict legal and penal action.

full_text:
NEW DELHI: AAP turncoat and BJP MP Raghav Chadha on Thursday broke his prolonged silence on the paper leak issue, speaking for the first time from the ruling side in Rajya Sabha. As BJP pushed the anti-paper leak Bill in the Parliament, Chadha said he did not want headlines but spoke "wholeheartedly in support of the students of India," adding that "PM Modi heard it just like the head of a family listens."
Chadha stressed that the paper leak crisis could only be resolved through an "institutional solution" and not through "media sound-bytes", which he claimed was the approach adopted by the PM Modi-led government.
BJP leader said, "I don't want headline, but an outcome."Addressing NEET aspirants, he said, "Your anger is justified. Your pain is real. And your concerns about the examination system are genuine."He further said that when students raised their voices in protest, the Prime Minister listened and acted as a "guardian" to address their concerns."Students demanded, the government acted. Historic decisions taken. System changed," Chadha said.
He also said that the government "heard and delivered."Highlighting the impact of paper leaks on students, he added, "Because a paper leak does not merely compromise an examination. It can wipe out years of preparation in a single moment."He further said, "Every student deserves an examination system where hard work and merit, not a leaked paper, decide the result."
Months ago, Chadha led a rebel exodus from Arvind Kejriwal-founded AAP, with seven Rajya Sabha members from the party breaking away and merging their faction with the ruling BJP.However, the Bill came under sharp criticism from the Opposition in the Rajya Sabha. Congress president Mallikarjun Kharge led the attack after Union minister Jitendra Singh tabled the Bill in the Upper House.Parliament Thursday approved the Public Examination (Prevention of Unfair Means) Amendment Bill, 2026, introducing stricter penalties for paper leaks and exam-related malpractices. The government said the legislation addresses one of the biggest concerns affecting students and called for cooperation from all stakeholders to tackle the issue.The Bill was passed by a voice vote in the Rajya Sabha amid an opposition walkout, a day after it cleared the Lok Sabha.
Under the amended law, individuals found guilty of paper leaks or other unfair means in public examinations will face a minimum prison term of five years, extendable to 10 years, along with a fine of up to Rs 50 lakh.For organised exam-related crimes, the Bill prescribes a minimum jail term of seven years and a fine of up to Rs 10 crore.The legislation also empowers state governments and Union Territory administrations to designate Courts of Session as special fast-track courts to try offences under the Act. These courts will conduct day-to-day proceedings and complete trials within three months of the filing of the chargesheet.

Amit Shah presented Lokmanya Tilak award to Ajit Doval and hailed his role in India's national security
NEW DELHI: Union home minister Amit Shah on Saturday lauded National Security Advisor (NSA) Ajit Doval for his contribution to India's national security and foreign policy, saying the veteran intelligence officer has played a crucial role behind every major national security decision taken by Prime Minister Narendra Modi since 2014.Speaking at a function in Pune after presenting the Lokmanya Tilak National Award 2026 to Doval, Shah said the NSA's advice and strategic inputs have been instrumental in strengthening India's security architecture and defence preparedness.He also said Doval's contribution to India's internal and external security had been so significant that history would reserve "a golden page" for him.
"NSA Ajit Doval has played a great role in strengthening India's foreign policy. In every decision of PM Modi for national security, Doval has had a 'role and advice' in the background," Shah said."Whenever history is written, if anyone analyses internal security and external security, then clearly, for Ajit Doval ji, a golden page will have to be kept reserved; there is no doubt about this," he added.
'First selection' after Modi became PM
Shah said one of the first decisions taken by PM Modi after assuming office in 2014 was appointing Doval as the National Security Advisor, a move he said transformed India's strategic posture.
"Today, India's foreign policy has become a foreign policy with a backbone of steel; no one can deny this. We have, along with self-respect, strengthened our position in the world," Shah said.Praising Doval's decades-long career in the Intelligence Bureau, Shah said India has emerged as a stronger and more confident nation under Modi's leadership, with Doval making a significant contribution to that transformation.
"After becoming NSA in 2014, Doval helped implement many strategic ideas on the ground and played a major role in modernising India's armed forces, strengthening technology, enhancing operational capability and improving the country's defence preparedness," Shah said.He added that the Modi government has fundamentally transformed both the defensive and offensive capabilities of the armed forces over the past 12 years, with Doval playing a key role in the process.Shah also noted that much of Doval's contribution can never be made public because of the confidential nature of intelligence operations.Recalling his tenure as Gujarat's home minister, Shah narrated how he first interacted with Doval following the Ahmedabad serial bomb blasts. He said then chief minister Narendra Modi had advised Gujarat Police to consult Doval while investigating the attacks."I remember Ajit ji had come to my house. The tips he gave resulted in Gujarat Police resolving not just the Ahmedabad bomb blast, but 13 bomb blasts across the country all at once. This was a very great achievement," Shah said.
Shah invokes Lokmanya Tilak's legacy
The Union home minister also paid tribute to Lokmanya Bal Gangadhar Tilak, calling him one of the foremost architects of India's freedom movement.He said Tilak's iconic slogan, "Swarajya is my birthright, and I shall have it," gave a new direction to India's freedom struggle and inspired generations of freedom fighters.
Shah added that the slogan made Indians realise that self-rule was their right and not a favour bestowed by anyone.Describing Tilak as a fearless journalist, Shah said one could truly understand courage in journalism only by reading the articles published in Kesari, the newspaper founded by the freedom fighter."How fearless a journalist can be can only be experienced by reading the articles of Kesari," he said.
Referring to Tilak's role in mobilising people through the public Ganesh and Shivaji festivals, Shah said they laid the foundation for cultural nationalism and that India continues to follow the path envisioned by the freedom fighter."India is now moving firmly on the path of cultural nationalism laid down by Lokmanya Bal Gangadhar Tilak, and no one can reverse that journey," he said.Shah further added that Tilak's ideas on nationalism, self-rule and social awakening continue to guide the country and remain relevant for nation-building, particularly for the younger generation.
Shah said honours such as the Lokmanya Tilak National Award are not merely ceremonial but recognise those who dedicate their lives to the country and inspire future generations."When such individuals are honoured, the feeling of gratitude of society towards them is discharged... Today, the Tilak Award that has been conferred upon Ajit Doval ji... for those who live for this country and work for this country, it will become a place of great inspiration," he said.
Doval accepts award with humility
Accepting the Lokmanya Tilak National Award, Doval thanked the organisers and said he was honoured to receive an award named after Lokmanya Tilak."I am thankful for this award named after Lokmanya Bal Gangadhar Tilak and accept it with humility," Doval said.Doval also praised the country's leadership, saying, "We are very fortunate to have leaders like PM Modi and Amit Shah".

NEW DELHI: India has screened 10,974 international travellers arriving from Ebola-affected countries since May 23 after the World Health Organization declared the Bundibugyo Ebola outbreak a Public Health Emergency of International Concern (PHEIC), with no case detected in the country so far, the Centre informed Parliament on Friday.The government said surveillance and preparedness were intensified across the country following the WHO declaration, with enhanced screening at airports and other points of entry, mandatory travel declarations, designated isolation facilities, expanded laboratory capacity and nationwide mock drills to prepare for any suspected case.
According to the ministry of health and family welfare, all international passengers are screened for recent travel to Democratic Republic of Congo, Uganda and South Sudanâcountries affected by the Ebola outbreak. The government has not imposed a blanket travel ban, but passengers with travel history to these countries during the previous 21 days are identified through Self Declaration Forms, including the Air Suvidha 2.0 portal.Mumbai accounted for the highest number of screened passengers at 7,568, followed by Delhi (1,833), Hyderabad (532), Chennai (210), Bengaluru (205) and Ahmedabad (200). At the state level, Gujarat recorded the highest number of screened passengers (2,905), followed by Maharashtra (2,228), Uttar Pradesh (785), Tamil Nadu (731), Telangana (624) and Kerala (554).
Replying to a question in the Lok Sabha, Union Health Minister J P Nadda said the Centre had coordinated its response with the National Centre for Disease Control (NCDC), Indian Council of Medical Research (ICMR), Directorate General of Health Services (DGHS), Ministry of Civil Aviation and other agencies to strengthen surveillance and preparedness.
The preparedness measures include issuing standard operating procedures covering surveillance, quarantine, laboratory testing, infection prevention and clinical management; identifying and operationalising isolation facilities across states and Union Territories; expanding diagnostic capacity through ICMR-NIV Pune and additional Biosafety Level-3 laboratories; deploying additional doctors and paramedical staff at major international airports; and conducting mock drills in designated hospitals nationwide.The government has also strengthened public awareness through airport displays, in-flight announcements, social media campaigns and a 24Ã7 national helpline while activating the NCDC Public Health Emergency Operations Centre to coordinate the response.The health ministry said no Ebola case has been reported in India so far.

NEW DELHI: Jammu and Kashmir chief minister Omar Abdullah on Saturday announced an ex gratia payment of Rs 10 lakh each for the families of two migrant labourers from Chhattisgarh who were killed in a terrorist attack at a brick kiln in Kulgam district.The attack took place late on Friday evening in the Kelam area of south Kashmir, where unidentified gunmen opened fire on the workers. Bhupendra, from Chhuiya village in Sarangarh-Bilaigarh district, had reached Kashmir around three months ago with his wife.

NEW DELHI: SC judge Ujjal Bhuyan has questioned opacity in the collegiumâs decisions on judicial appointments.âI have noticed that the last three collegium resolutions contain no reasons whatsoever. Is this a step back from the principle of transparency?â said Justice Bhuyan at a panel discussion on Saturday. âBy withholding reasons, we also create space for individuals to enter the judiciary who may later describe groups of people as âantsâ and make other remarks that are wholly unconstitutional,â he said.Citizens have right to know deliberations on elevation, transfer of judges: BhuyanTo prevent the entry of such people, âthere should be some discussion, there should be some reasons givenâ, said Justice Ujjal Bhuyan. Though the judge didnât name anyone, the comment was an apparent reference to a remark by an Allahabad high court judge at a social event in 2024.He was speaking at the launch of the Judicial Transparency Index: Assessing Disclosure of Information by the Supreme Court and the High Courts, prepared by the Justice, Access and Lowering Delays in India (JALDI) Initiative at the Vidhi Centre for Legal Policy.The judge stressed that deliberations on the elevation and transfer of judges by the SC collegium largely remain confidential, contrary to the principle of judicial transparency.
âWhile carrying out the next assessment on the scale of Judicial Transparency Index, I may request the JALDI team to also look into the aspect of opacity of the collegium system. Deliberations on elevation and transfer of judges remain confidential. Reasons for rejecting or deferring a recommendation are rarely disclosed in full. And the criteria applied are not codified in any publicly disclosed instrument. It is a very important issue. Citizens have a right to know what is happening in the courts. They have a right to know who would be their judges.They have a right to know judgments. These should be in the public domainâ, Justice Bhuyan underlined.The report is the first systematic study assessing transparency practices across Indiaâs higher judiciary and evaluates disclosure of information by the Supreme Court and high courts across judicial processes, institutional governance and administration, and judicial and administrative personnel.Referring to a previous collegium resolution reiterating the recommendation of senior advocate Saurabh Kirpal for appointment as a judge, Justice Bhuyan said he found the reasons recorded by the Supreme Court convincing but noted that despite more than three and a half years having passed, no appointment materialised.

NEW DELHI: GST collections rose 15.4% to Rs 2,11,205 crore in July, the second highest since the new structure was implemented last Sept, on the back of a 29% jump in integrated GST (IGST) on imports. This was also the highest pace of growth since rate rationalisation.The rise in IGST on imports in July (for transactions in the previous month) may be attributed to higher prices of crude and other commodities in the wake of the West Asia conflict.The impact of strong economic activity in June, when factory output grew at its fastest pace in nearly two years, was also visible on the tax numbers, seen as an advance indicator of economic activity. Some of the price hikes in FMCG and automobile sectors would have also buoyed collections. Central GST mop-up was pegged 12.3% higher at just under Rs 40,000 crore, while state GST grew 8.7% to nearly Rs 48,000 crore."The high GST collections tie in very well with the 7.3% increase in industrial production during June. It reflects continued economic resilience despite the challenges in the external environment...The
steady growth in GST collections each month indicates that overall domestic consumption is becoming largely insulated from seasonal variations and external headwinds," said MS Mani, partner at Deloitte India.Some experts, however, are worried about the continued rise in imports. "...one cannot ignore the elevated levels of import GST collections, which remain a nagging concern. This points to a persistent gap in domestic manufacturing capability despite the range of successful PLI and Atmanirbhar Bharat interventions rolled out over the past few years.
It is likely that the sustained push by policymakers towards localisation of around 100 products (being talked about) over a period of time will help bridge this gap," said Saurabh Agarwal, partner at EY India, a consulting firm.Net of refunds, which were 13% higher at almost Rs 30,000 crore, collections went up 15.8% to Rs 1,81,237 crore.Haryana logged the highest growth of 28%, followed by Gujarat and Puducherry (26%), Karnataka and Goa (23%), and Maharashtra (20%). Chhattisgarh (23% fall), Jharkhand and Manipur (20% decline) were among the laggards.

full_text:
Walk into any diagnostics lab in a major Indian city and you will likely be handed a laminated menu, not of food, but of the body. Silver package, gold package, platinum package. Forty tests, sixty tests, ninety. Fasting blood sugar, thyroid panels, vitamin D, cardiac markers, tumour markers, all bundled together and priced to feel like a bargain rather than a medical decision. Nobody asks whether these tests were prescribed by a doctor, because increasingly, they aren't. They are sold.This is the quieter side of India's healthcare story, one that gets far less attention than the shortage of hospital beds or the scarcity of rural doctors. In the country's cities, among its insured and upwardly mobile, a different problem has taken root: too much testing, too often, for too little reason. Corporate wellness programmes hand out annual full-body checkups as a perk. Insurance companies fold preventive panels into premium plans as a selling point. Diagnostic chains run festive discounts on scans the way electronics stores discount televisions. The result is a population of healthy, asymptomatic people walking out with reports listing dozens of parameters, several flagged in borderline yellow, and no doctor in the room to explain what any of it means.
The consequences are not trivial. Overtesting drives a cascade, a mildly abnormal number on an unnecessary test leads to a follow-up scan, which leads to a biopsy, which leads to weeks of anxiety over something that may never have caused harm.Doctors describe patients arriving with thick folders of test results and no clinical complaint, unsure why they were tested in the first place, but certain that more tests must mean better health.The question this raises is not whether early detection saves lives, it does, but whether India's growing test-industrial complex has confused detection with reassurance, and reassurance with health.
When does a test actually become necessary?
Ask a doctor practising evidence-based medicine when a test is warranted, and the answer rarely begins with the test itself. It begins with a conversation."It's an individualised question," says Dr. Haripriya Jagadish, Internal Medicine Specialist at Apollo Spectra Hospital, Chennai. "Most practitioners go by evidence-based medicine. The doctor will elicit the history, which will include all the symptoms of the patient, and based on that, the tests are done."That process, history-taking, is the part of clinical practice most invisible to the patient and most absent from the retail model of testing. A doctor working through a patient's symptoms, duration, family history and risk factors is, in effect, narrowing a list of possibilities before ordering a single test, so that each test serves to confirm or rule out something specific. A preventive package sold off a billboard skips that step entirely, running dozens of tests without first asking what, if anything, the patient's body is signalling.
India's overtesting epidemic (AI generated image)
According to Dr Jagadish, the reasons a test is actually indicated tend to fall into a few well-defined categories. "The common reasons start from infections, chronic diseases, inflammation and malignancy," she says. "Everything is based on the symptoms and the science." An unexplained fever might point toward an infection workup. Unexplained fatigue or weight change, paired with family history, might justify screening for a chronic condition such as diabetes or thyroid dysfunction. Persistent, localised pain or an abnormal finding on physical examination might warrant investigation for inflammation or, in some cases, malignancy. In each instance, the test follows the symptom, not the other way around.This is the clinical logic that preventive test packages tend to bypass. Rather than starting with a patient's history and narrowing toward a hypothesis, they start with a menu of everything available and work backward, hoping that volume compensates for the absence of a clinical question. For Dr. Jagadish's generation of evidence-based practitioners, that inversion is precisely the problem, not that testing itself is harmful, but that testing without a preceding clinical reason strips it of the context needed to interpret what the results actually mean.
Regulation that hasn't caught up
When a pharmaceutical company in India wants to advertise a prescription drug to the public, the law steps in, such advertising is restricted, and in most cases requires government authorisation before it can run. When a diagnostics chain wants to advertise a bundle of forty preventive tests, including several with genuine cancer-screening implications, no equivalent threshold exists. The test package occupies a regulatory blind spot: not quite a drug, not quite a medical procedure requiring a prescription, and therefore largely free to be marketed the way any consumer product would be, with discounts, urgency, and appeals to fear.India's oversight of diagnostic laboratories does exist, but it is aimed almost entirely at technical quality, accreditation bodies set standards for how accurately a lab must run a test, not for whether that test should have been sold to an asymptomatic customer in the first place, or how the results should be communicated once they arrive. There is no requirement that a preventive test package be accompanied by pre-test counselling, no mandate that a qualified clinician interpret results before they reach the patient, and no restriction on marketing screening tests directly to consumers with no clinical indication.This is not a uniquely Indian problem, direct-to-consumer testing has expanded globally, and regulators in some markets have begun responding, tightening requirements around what claims these tests can make and how aggressively they can be marketed to healthy people. What distinguishes India is the pace of that catch-up. As the market for retail diagnostics has scaled rapidly across metros and now smaller cities, the regulatory apparatus governing how these tests are sold, and to whom, has largely stayed where it was decades ago, built for an era when a blood test still required a doctor to ask for it.
The anxiety economy
The report itself rarely arrives with context. It arrives as a PDF or a printed sheet, rows of values, reference ranges in brackets, and a handful highlighted in red or yellow, with no accompanying explanation of what those deviations actually mean for a specific person's health. For a patient with no symptoms and no clinical history prompting the test, that ambiguity becomes fertile ground for anxiety.The pattern is a familiar one to clinicians. A mildly elevated tumour marker, a borderline nodule on an incidental scan, a number just outside the "normal" range on a test that was never clinically indicated in the first place, these findings, once flagged, tend to set off a cascade. The patient seeks a specialist opinion. The specialist, unable to rule out concern from a single data point, orders a follow-up scan or a repeat test. In some cases, that escalates further to a biopsy or invasive procedure, undertaken to investigate a finding that may have had no clinical significance to begin with.
The anxiety economy (AI generated image)
Dr Jagadish points to this as one of the central risks of indiscriminate testing. "The problem with getting too many tests, especially ones like cancer screening, is when you do them and get an abnormal value, unless there's a medical correlation, it can do more harm than good," she says. "Especially this generation has a lot of anxiety around that. It unnecessarily drives up the medical cost of the patient as well as the psychological trauma."That psychological toll rarely features in conversations about overtesting, which tend to focus on financial waste or clinical inefficiency. But for the patient sitting with an unexplained abnormal result, the experience is rarely just administrative. It is weeks of uncertainty, repeated consultations, and a growing preoccupation with a number that may resolve on its own, or may never have meant anything at all. For a generation already primed toward health anxiety, amplified by symptom-checking apps, wellness content and a culture that treats more data as inherently reassuring, an unexplained flagged result can be harder to sit with than the absence of information ever was.
What gets lost in this cycle is the fact that not every abnormality requires action. Medicine has long understood that some findings are incidental, present, but clinically irrelevant, yet a system that tests first and interprets later leaves little room for that nuance. The result is a quiet, largely undocumented cost of overtesting: not just money spent on unnecessary follow-ups, but the accumulated weight of worry carried by people who were never actually sick.

NEW DELHI: Exiled Bangladeshi author Taslima Nasreen on Saturday described her return to India after nearly two decades as proof that âinjustice can be long but cannot be permanent.âShe made the remarks at an event in Kolkata, nearly two decades after she was forced to leave the city in 2007. The 63-year-old writer had been living in Kolkata since leaving Bangladesh in 1994 amid alleged death threats from radical groups over her writings and views on religion.Nasreen, who has been living in Europe since leaving Kolkata, also clarified that her return to the city was not linked to any "political agenda.""Today, the opening of this door proves that injustice can be long, but it cannot be permanent. History remembers who closed the doors and who opened them...I am not here to speak for any political party, or against any party. I am here to speak in favour of women's rights," PTI quoted her as saying.She also expressed concern over what she described as a "rise" in religious extremism in Bangladesh."I am against all forms of fundamentalism, but I have spoken against Islamic fundamentalists because I have seen it from close quarters since childhood.
The rise of fundamentalism in Bangladesh is at an alarming stage. Freedom of speech is being curtailed," Nasreen said.Visibly emotional, Nasreen called her return a "fulfilment of a long-awaited moment.""It took me 19 years to say these words: 'I have returned to Kolkata.' I felt the pain of losing an address every single day. On August 8, 1994, the then government forced me to leave Bangladesh. The state may have removed me from my country, but it could never remove my country from within me," she added.Lamenting that she could not find a permanent home in either Bangladesh or West Bengal, Nasreen highlighted that Europe had provided her security but not a sense of belonging."Europe has given me citizenship and a place to live, but unfortunately, I couldn't get a small place to stay in the two Bengals. Europe gave me security, but it could not give me a sense of belonging. A home is not built by security alone; it is built by language, memory and culture," Nasreen remarked.Nasreen maintained that she had never been convicted by any court but had faced restrictions because of opposition from fundamentalist groups."I committed no crime. No court has ever punished me. It is a painful truth of our times that a writer needs police protection to visit the city of her own language."
Rejecting allegations that her writings were offensive, she emphasised that her advocacy had focused on equality and human rights."I only spoke about equal rights for women and men, and about human rights irrespective of religion or caste. I said that any rule or doctrine that takes away equality and human dignity must be changed."She also criticised what she described as the unequal treatment of women in the name of religion and backed a Uniform Civil Code across South Asia, arguing that religion-based personal laws discriminate against women."The real conflict is between secularism and fundamentalism, between the rational mind and irrationality, between innovation and tradition, and between people who value freedom and those who do not."

Border trade through the Nathula Pass in East Sikkim, a key segment of the ancient Silk Route connecting India and China, resumed on Saturday after remaining suspended for nearly six years. A formal reopening ceremony was held at Nathula, with officials from both countries participating in the event.The trade route had remained closed since 2020 due to the Covid-19 pandemic and subsequent border tensions between India and China.Welcoming the resumption of trade, Anil Gupta, General Secretary of the Indo-China Nathula Border Traders Welfare Association, thanked Sikkim Chief Minister Prem Singh Tamang for his efforts in facilitating the reopening.
"I extend heartfelt thanks to our Chief Minister, Prem Singh Tamang. This has become possible today solely due to his efforts. For traders who had outstanding dues or stocks stranded on the other side, this is a time of great joy, and everyone is happy," Gupta said.
Traders seek expansion of trade list
While welcoming the resumption of trade, Gupta said the existing list of goods permitted through Nathula needs to be updated to reflect present-day commercial needs.
"The current trading list includes items like horses, sheep and general goods. We believe industrial products relevant to today's times should be included. We have submitted a formal request to the department, and we are hopeful that the government will take a very positive view of this," he said.
Under the existing arrangement, only a limited list of traditional goods is allowed to be traded through the border route. Traders have long been seeking the inclusion of industrial and other commercially relevant products.

NEW DELHI: The Centre has announced a series of changes for the NEET-PG exam to be held later in the month, including expanding the choice of test locations, giving candidates more time to plan travel, and increasing the time available per question.The reforms are aimed at making the National Eligibility-cum-Entrance Test for Postgraduate (NEET-PG) process more convenient and secure, according to the Union health ministry.Under the revised system, candidates will have to provide preferences for three states for their examination centre. Their correspondence state will be the mandatory first preference, allowing allotment of centres closer to their place of residence.Earlier, examination centres were allotted on a first-come, first-served basis, prompting candidates to submit applications immediately after registrations opened. Those who delayed often found nearby centres unavailable and had to travel to other states.Candidates will now be informed of their allotted test city nearly three weeks before the August 30 examination, giving them more time to arrange travel and accommodation.
The National Board of Examinations in Medical Sciences (NBEMS) has also revised the exam pattern, reducing the number of questions from 200 to 180 while keeping the total duration unchanged at 210 minutes. The move will provide candidates with more time per question.The exam was earlier conducted with 200 multiple-choice questions carrying a maximum of 800 marks.The ministry said the question paper preparation and delivery process has been strengthened through multiple layers of encryption, secure offline preparation, time-bound finalisation of papers shortly before the examination, and controlled digital decryption at the start of the test.To further strengthen security, Aadhaar-based authentication has been introduced during registration and on the examination day. Iris-based biometric verification will be used where fingerprint authentication fails.NBEMS has also introduced a dedicated email address for reporting impersonation, touting and other unfair practices, while issuing advisories to candidates to improve awareness and vigilance.NEET-PG 2026 will be conducted in a single shift to ensure uniformity in difficulty level and assessment. In recent years, the exam was conducted in multiple shifts due to emergencies or postponements.Union health minister JP Nadda on Saturday reviewed preparations for the examination and directed agencies to ensure a smooth, secure, transparent and technology-enabled process. He assessed the readiness of NBEMS, technology partners and other stakeholders, and stressed the need for a fair and candidate-friendly examination.
A total of 2,73,183 candidates have registered for the medical entrance test, an increase of over 12.5% from last year. The exam will be held in a single shift across around 340 cities and more than 1,300 centres.Security measures include advance sealing and verification of centres, CCTV surveillance, biometric authentication, candidate frisking, deployment of signal jammers, live monitoring through central and regional command centres, and supervision by independent observers and appraisers.More than 60,000 examination functionaries will be deployed for the smooth conduct of the examination, the ministry said.(With PTI inputs)

Indiaâs monsoon has delivered a surprise this July, defying forecasts of below-normal rainfall despite a strengthening El Nino and reinforcing scientistsâ warnings that climate change is altering the countryâs most important weather system, report Chittaranjan Tembhekar & Gaurav Talwar.As of July 30, India received 270.1mm of rains in July against a normal of 271.9mm, well within normal range. IMD had said July rainfall was likely to be less than 94% of long period average.
However, rainfall distribution remained skewed, with central India receiving 29% excess in July while the east & northeast recorded a deficit of 30% and south 28%.The monsoon deficit since June 1 was 14%. The unexpected turnaround in July has eased fears of a big monsoon shortfall but highlighted a new reality: long dry spells interspersed with short bursts of extremely heavy rain capable of triggering floods and landslides.
El NiÃ±o alone can no more explain Indiaâs rain pattern: Experts
According to a Climate Trends briefing, successive weather systems cut the national rainfall deficit considerably from 40% at the end of June.Scientists say the biggest lesson from monsoon 2026 is that El NiÃ±o alone can no longer explain Indiaâs rainfall behaviour.Global warming, warming oceans and changing atmospheric circulation are increasingly interacting with traditional climate drivers, making monsoon forecasts more difficult.
âThe challenge is no longer predicting how much rain India will receive, but forecasting where, when and how intensely it will fall in a warming climate,â scientists said.Rainfall remained highly uneven. While 16 meteorological subdivisions states recorded normal rainfall in the season and three saw excess to large-excess rainfall, 17 subdivisions remained deficient. Central India was almost normal with a 1% surplus, northwest India had an 11% shortfall, while east and northeast India remained 30% below normal and south India 25% deficient.The findings are particularly striking because the US National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration has projected an 81% probability of a very strong El NiÃ±o developing between Oct and Dec â a pattern usually associated with weaker Indian monsoons.
Former IMD director general K J Ramesh attributed Julyâs recovery to abnormal warming over the western Pacific, which spawned successive monsoon systems over the Bay of Bengal, and the increasing influence of Western Disturbances that enhanced rainfall over Maharashtra and Gujarat.âClimate change is reshaping the characteristics of the monsoon, which existing models are failing to take into account,â Ramesh said.Akshay Deoras of the University of Reading said the monsoon rebounded rapidly after an early July lull. He cited Umbergaon in Gujarat receiving 1,064 mm of rain in 24 hours âamong the highest daily totals recorded since 1901 â as evidence of intensifying rainfall extremes, adding that climate change appears to be amplifying the monsoonâs internal weather systems.

NEW DELHI: Prime Minister Narendra Modi on Saturday inaugurated the Swami Vivekananda Cultural Youth Centre â Viveka Smaraka in Karnataka's Mysuru, describing it as a centre that would inspire young Indians to embrace the ideals of nation-building, service and character development.The Prime Minister was accompanied by Karnataka chief minister DK Shivakumar during the inauguration.Before unveiling the centre, PM Modi visited the Viveka Smaraka, offered prayers, planted a sapling on the premises and watched a short film on the life, teachings and legacy of Swami Vivekananda.
The youth centre has been built by the Sri Ramakrishna Ashrama, Mysuru, at the site where Swami Vivekananda stayed during his visit to Mysuru in November 1892, a visit regarded as significant because it was here that he first decided to participate in the World's Parliament of Religions in Chicago in 1893.
'Youth strength is driving India's growth'
Addressing the gathering, PM Modi said India's future depended on empowering young people through education, opportunities and confidence to achieve their aspirations within the country."In any country, the potential of the youth transforms into national strength only when they receive the right opportunities and direction, and the confidence to dream big and realise those dreams on their own soil. Our educational institutions play a pivotal role in this regard," the Prime Minister said.
Highlighting the government's focus on higher education, PM Modi said India now has around 1.4 lakh MBBS seats, while the number of medical colleges has increased to 823.
He also said the National Education Policy (NEP) was preparing Indian youth for the demands of the 21st century."The youth of India, once in chains, today are accelerating the world's development. Today, India's economy is growing at the fastest pace because of the strength of India's youth. Today, India has the world's third-largest startup ecosystem because of the strength of India's youth," PM Modi said.
PM Modi recalls Swami Vivekananda's connection with Mysuru
The Prime Minister said Mysuru held a special place in Swami Vivekananda's life and described the city as a centre of India's cultural consciousness."Today on this sacred land of Mysuru, I am experiencing a different kind of energy. I humbly bow at the feet of all saints. Mysuru has been a centre of India's ancient cultural consciousness. India's heritage is ingrained in every part of this city," he said.Recalling Vivekananda's visit more than 130 years ago, PM Modi said the then Maharaja of Mysuru recognised the young monk's potential and extended support to him."Mysuru played an important role in the life of Swami Vivekananda ji. About 130 years ago, Swami ji, as a young monk, came to Mysuru while travelling. Among those who recognised him then and associated with him, a prominent name is that of the then Maharaja of Mysuru. When Swami Vivekananda ji was in America, he wrote a letter from there to the then Maharaja of Mysuru. In it, he himself mentioned the Maharaja's support," PM Modi said.He added that the government was modernising educational infrastructure and reshaping the education system to meet emerging requirements.
'Viveka Smaraka will inspire generations'
Calling the newly inaugurated centre a future hub for spiritual and cultural learning, PM Modi expressed confidence that it would become a destination for young people seeking inspiration from Swami Vivekananda's ideals."I am confident that the Viveka Smaraka will become a pilgrimage site for spiritual upliftment for seekers and devotees," he said.

Youth for whom 'Nation First' is the supreme guiding principle, and whose life's mission is the service of Mother India," PM Modi said.

NEW DELHI: The Bombay high court on Friday came down heavily on Indians who litter public places at home but follow cleanliness rules abroad, saying the same people who "throw garbage on the road without batting an eyelid" in India ensure to put "even a small chocolate wrapper" in the dustbin abroad.The court stressed that maintaining cleanliness is a fundamental duty and called for strict action against offenders.A bench of Justices G S Kulkarni and Aarti Sathe made the observations while hearing a batch of petitions over pollution, foul odour, gas emissions and health hazards linked to the Kanjurmarg dumping ground in Mumbai.The judges said public participation was essential to keeping the city clean and urged civic authorities to enforce the rules without hesitation."If a person wants a clean environment, then he or she has a corresponding fundamental duty towards society to maintain cleanliness. Here, a person will throw garbage on the road without batting an eyelid, but these same people, when abroad, will strictly avoid such behaviour.
Even a small chocolate wrapper they will throw in the dustbin," the high court said.The bench then questioned, "Is this the price of liberty and democracy?"The court also voiced concern over the large quantity of plastic waste strewn across public places, observing that even Mumbai's beaches are littered with plastic. "It is in these circumstances the role of MCGM's cleanliness machinery wardwise becomes significant, to take all effective steps so that public streets are not used by the citizens as dumping places," the bench observed.The court said failing to enforce the rules would defeat the objective behind the civic body's cleanliness campaign and urged authorities to implement the existing regulations strictly.It also raised concerns over the handling of garbage near heritage landmarks such as Rajabai Tower and the Bombay high court building. NEW DELHI: Bringing the six-year-long trial in the murder of Intelligence Bureau staffer Ankit Sharma to a close, a Delhi court on Friday sentenced former AAP councillor Tahir Hussain and four others to life imprisonment, holding that Sharma was lynched âsolely on account of his religionâ during the 2020 northeast Delhi riots.Additional sessions judge Parveen Kumar Singh, however, declined the prosecutionâs plea for the death penalty, ruling that while the brutality of the crime was undeniable, the prosecution had failed to prove any specific act committed by each convict during the murder.
Pronouncing the sentence, Singh described the murder as one of exceptional brutality committed during the âcommunal violence that erupted in the wake of the protests against CAA/NRCâ.The court held that the prosecution failed to prove allegations that Hussain had âaided, abetted, instigated or led the unlawful assemblyâ. Singh rejected the other convictsâ pleas that they were sole breadwinners. However, he did consider their educational background as a mitigating factor.On July 13, the court had convicted Hussain and four others, holding that the five were part of âa large crowd which, with animus against Hindus, had assembled...
with a common object to commit rioting, loot, arson and to cause damage to the property and person of members of the Hindu communityâ, before murdering the IB staffer on Feb 25, 2020, whose body was later recovered from a drain.
'Only death sentence will be justiceâHussain was sentenced to six monthsâ RI under IPC Section 188, three years under Section 153A, two years under Section 147, three years under Section 148, seven years under Section 365 and imprisonment for life under Section 302. All sentences will run concurrently. He was also fined Rs 1,000 under Section 188, Rs 20,000 each under Sections 153A, 147 and 148, Rs 50,000 under Section 365 and Rs 5 lakh under Section 302, with default sentences in case of non-payment.âThe manner in which it was committed was of the utmost brutality. The victim was sucked in by the murderous mob, baying for blood... The assault was so fierce, unrelenting, and from such close quarters that even in death, the body did not immediately slump to the ground,â the judge held.The court noted that the violence did not end with Sharmaâs death. His body, it observed, was strapped âlike an animalâ, dragged to Chand Bagh pulia and thrown into a drain. Calling it an âaggravating circumstance of immense magnitudeâ, the judge remarked, âAs if the hatred had still not been satiated, the dead body was thereafter thrown into the nala. Therefore, the barbarity with which this horrendous murder was committed is nauseatingly sickening.âSaying the âcrime testâ tilted the case towards the ârarest of rareâ category, the judge weighed aggravating and mitigating circumst-ances before declining the capital punishment sought by special public prosecutor Madhukar Pandey, who maintained that the offence was part of âwell-orchestrated communal violenceâ rather than a crime committed und-er sudden provocation.The court zoomed in on what it found to be the prosecutionâs principal shortcoming â the lack of specificity regarding the individual role of each convict. Observing that âbefore a life is ordered to be extinguished by a judicial decreeâ, something more than mere membership of an unlawful assembly had to be proved, the judge held that the prosecution had failed to bridge that gap. While acknowledging the stateâs contention that the use of a heavy cutting weapon reflected pre-planned and cold-blooded intent, the court said the time for drawing such inferences was long past and treated the lack of specificity as a âhuge mitigation.âJudge Singh rejected the convictsâ pleas that they were sole breadwinners and noted that the âmonstrosity of the crime committed outweighs this mitigating circumstanceâ. At the same time, he found no material to conclude that they were beyond reform.It also noted that allegations of Hussainâs house being used as a âlaunchpadâ for the riots were neither part of the charges framed nor specifically proved during trial. All the sentences will run concurrently.
As Hussain was being led out of the courtroom by police after the sentencing, he turned to those present and said, âHigh court se insaaf milega. Der aaye, lekin durust aaye.âSpeaking to TOI, Ankur Sharma, brother of the IB staffer, said, âFrom day one, this has been a ârarest of rareâ case. The sheer brutality of the crime still haunts our family every single day; knowing he was inflicted with 51 wounds, subjected to acid, and dumped in a drain is a pain that never truly goes away.â

NEW DELHI: The Supreme Court on Friday granted interim protection from arrest to DMK leader and former Tamil Nadu minister V Senthil Balaji in the alleged TASMAC corruption case. The court directed Balaji to deposit his passport, cooperate with the investigation and refrain from influencing witnesses while granting him relief.A Bench of Chief Justice of India Surya Kant and Justice Joymalya Bagchi stayed the operation of FIR No. 05 of 2026 and issued notice to the Tamil Nadu government on Balaji's plea challenging the Madras high court's refusal to grant anticipatory bail."Subject to the petitioner fully cooperating with the probe, his arrest shall remain stayed. He is directed to deposit his passport with the Investigating Officer. FIR No. 05 of 2026 dated July 8 shall remain stayed. He shall not attempt to influence witnesses," the Bench directed, ANI reported.The FIR was registered by the Directorate of Vigilance and Anti-Corruption (DVAC) following the Madras high court's refusal to grant anticipatory bail to Balaji in the alleged TASMAC scam involving purported irregularities in the allotment of liquor shops and bars.During the hearing, the Supreme Court questioned whether the police should have conducted a preliminary enquiry before registering the FIR, observing that it appeared to be based largely on an affidavit filed by the Enforcement Directorate (ED).
The Bench also noted that the allegations primarily related to the period between 2020 and 2021 and observed that Balaji was no longer a minister."He is no longer a Minister," the Court remarked, adding that "if an independent investigation found him guilty, he is bound to face consequences."Senior advocate Amit Anand Tiwari, appearing for Balaji along with senior advocates Kapil Sibal and Mukul Rohatgi, argued that custodial interrogation was unnecessary."Our contention is that the FIR is for the incident said to have taken place between 2021 and 2025. I am at no flight risk; no custodial interrogation required. I was the minister in the department and TASMAC is a corporation independent in existence and functioning," Tiwari submitted, according to PTI.Balaji also contended that the FIR substantially reproduced the Enforcement Directorate's affidavit and petition filed before the Supreme Court."In fact, the FIR itself at various places says that it is from the counter affidavit and petition of the ED," his plea stated.Opposing the plea, the Tamil Nadu government argued that Balaji continued to wield considerable influence despite no longer holding office."From 2021 to 2025, he was in power and did not let any complaint sustain against him. We will have a problem if the evidence goes away. Considering the kind of scam that has happened and his antecedents--there are at least six serious cases," the prosecution submitted.The State further argued, "Even if he is not in power, he is able to carry on the influence."Justice Bagchi, however, said the State's concerns could be addressed by imposing appropriate safeguards.
"He is not going to abscond, as you say. We will ensure that he does not abscond, participates in the investigation and does not interfere with the probe. If there is any breach, we will interfere," Justice Bagchi observed.
Chief Justice of India Surya Kant also stressed that the investigation should proceed independently."Hold an independent probe. If he is guilty, he will face..." the Chief Justice observed.While granting interim protection, Justice Bagchi cautioned Balaji's counsel that any violation of the conditions would invite immediate action.The Supreme Court's order came a day after senior advocates Kapil Sibal and Mukul Rohatgi sought an urgent hearing, arguing that Balaji faced imminent coercive action following the Madras high court's refusal to grant anticipatory bail.The case stems from allegations of a large-scale cash kickback scheme in TASMAC involving the allotment of liquor shops and bars.

[SEP] Thirukkural with the Times explores real-world lessons from the classic Tamil text âThirukkuralâ. Written by Tamil poet and philosopher Thiruvalluvar, the Kural consists of 1,330 short couplets of seven words each. This text is divided into three books with teachings on virtue, wealth, and love and is considered one of the great works ever on ethics and morality. The Kural has influenced scholars and leaders across social, political, and philosophical spheres.Motivational speaker, author and diversity champion Bharathi Bhaskar explores the masterpiece.There is a kind of ignorance that is harmless. Then there is another kind that troubles me deeply. It ridicules what it has never cared to learn. History, scholarship, art, music, literature and sacrifice become material for cheap amusement. The ancient Greeks called such people the Philistines. Whatever the label, the damage they cause is real.A recent television programme left me with precisely this feeling.It was presented as a comedy. Four young adults sat chatting casually. One participant asked the others, "Do you know V O C? What did he pull?"One participant guessed he must have been a boatman and therefore pulled a boat. Another remarked, "I thought he pulled a saree, like how Duryodhana did." In the Mahabharata, it was Dushasana, not Duryodhana, who dragged Draupadi's saree. The studio laughed.But who was really being laughed at?Not V O Chidambaram Pillai. It was our own history.V O C, revered as Kappalottiya Tamilan, challenged the British shipping monopoly by founding the Swadeshi Steam Navigation Company in 1906. When Indian merchants suffered under the colonial shipping monopoly, he dared to dream of Indian-owned ships to sail between Tuticorin and Colombo. He raised funds, purchased two ships and stood up to an empire.The British retaliated with brutal vengeance.Arrested on charges of sedition, he was sentenced to rigorous imprisonment. Inside the prison, this distinguished lawyer was yoked to an oil press, forced to perform labour meant for bullocks. Those agonising years earned him the title Sekkizhuththa Semmal. Poverty marked the rest of his life, but his sacrifice became a foundation for India's political and economic freedom.It was this extraordinary life that became a punchline.Ignorance is never a crime. Ridiculing greatness is.Psychologists David Dunning and Justin Kruger described this tendency in 1999. The Dunning-Kruger effect explains how people with very little knowledge often possess enormous confidence while failing to recognise genuine expertise.Perhaps that is why a classical musician, an accomplished dancer, a gifted artist, a poet, a scientist or a freedom fighter can become easy targets. Even in schools, children who excel in studies are sometimes mocked or bullied simply because they perform well. Such ridicule often grows from insecurity, resentment and the inability to appreciate another's excellence.Thiruvalluvar recognised this danger centuries ago. He devoted an entire chapter to Periyaarai Pizhaiyaamai. In Kural 896, he says:Eriyaal Sudappadinum Uyvuundaam; Uyyaar Periyaarp Pizhaithozhu VaarOne may escape from flames, but none escape the consequences of insulting the greatValluvar's wisdom does not stop with freedom fighters or celebrated personalities. It quietly crosses the threshold of our homes.How often do we see ageing parents or in-laws spoken to with impatience, mocked or dismissed as outdated? More painful still, how often do parents remain silent when their own children belittle grandparents? Respect for elders is not an old-fashioned custom. It is the moral foundation of every enduring culture. The day we begin laughing at those who carried us before we could walk, taught us before we could read and sacrificed before we could dream, we have diminished ourselves. A society that mocks its achievers, bullies its brightest children and humiliates its elders is not progressing. It has quietly vanquished its soul.
