India's un-employment crisis and helplessness of modern life. (Representative image)
Franz Kafka's The Metamorphosis transformed an ordinary man into a giant insect to explore alienation, helplessness and the dehumanising pressures of modern life.More than a century later, India's self-styled Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) has adopted a similarly unsettling symbol, not to tell a work of fiction, but to express the frustrations of a generation increasingly unsure whether years of education, expensive coaching and relentless competition will ever translate into a stable job.What began as a social media sensation with a strong and straightforward satirical structure, quickly evolved into one of the country's biggest youth-led movements in recent years.Calling itself the "voice of the lazy and unemployed," the movement grew from memes mocking joblessness, paper leaks, inflation and the political establishment into street protests.The protest may have become a trigger for a generation already grappling with shrinking employment opportunities, rising educational costs and growing uncertainty about the future.And at its heart lies a simple question. What happens when an economy produces millions of graduates every year but fails to create enough quality jobs?According to veteran economist Arun Kumar, a retired professor at JNU, "This unemployment crisis has created a huge gap between expectations and reality.""Young people earn degrees believing they will secure good jobs, but when those jobs do not materialise, they continue preparing for competitive examinations year after year. Many take these exams four, five or even six times because they still hope to secure an organised sector job.
Their parents also encourage them because they know such jobs offer stable salaries and social security," he said."But the increasing privatisation of education has intensified competition. Coaching institutes want to showcase high success rates because that is their biggest selling point. That creates incentives for unethical practices, including paper leaks. The greater the privatisation, the greater the pressure to resort to illegal methods to ensure students succeed. Fake degrees, cheating and question paper leaks are all symptoms of a much deeper problem. They are linked to unemployment and the shortage of quality jobs in the organised sector," he added.
India's employment challenge
India has spent decades expanding access to higher education. Universities have multiplied, enrollment has surged and millions of families have invested heavily in degrees, viewing education as the surest path to upward mobility.The numbers tell a remarkable story. According to the State of Working India 2026 report by Azim Premji University, the number of young graduates in India increased nearly 13-fold, rising from around 5 million in 1983 to 63 million in 2023.But while the supply of graduates has grown rapidly, employment opportunities have not kept pace.The report estimates that graduate unemployment among people below the age of 25 is now close to 40%, while graduates accounted for nearly two-thirds of India's unemployed population in 2023.Even more striking is the rise in the number of unemployed graduates, which has increased from less than one million in 1983 to around 11 million in 2023, a 16-fold increase over four decades.The mismatch between education and employment has widened steadily since the mid-2000s as higher education expanded much faster than the creation of quality jobs. For millions of families, earning a college degree no longer guarantees stable employment or financial security.Recent government data suggest that the challenge is becoming even more severe.According to the government's flagship Periodic Labour Force Survey (PLFS), unemployment among Indians aged 15 to 29 rose to 16.2% in June, the highest level recorded since monthly estimates became available in April 2025. At that time, youth unemployment stood at 13.8%.The ministry of statistics and programme implementation (MoSPI) has cautioned that monthly figures may fluctuate because of seasonal factors, academic cycles and the increased frequency of surveys. Even so, the latest numbers are significant because they fit into a broader pattern rather than representing an isolated spike. Youth unemployment has increased across all six categories tracked by the survey, urban and rural areas, men and women alike, during the 15 months for which monthly data are available.At the same time, the Labour Force Participation Rate (LFPR) among young people has declined from 42.7% to 40.3%. In simple terms, fewer young people are actively looking for work.Ordinarily, such a decline would be expected to reduce unemployment because fewer people are participating in the labour market. Instead, unemployment has continued to rise, suggesting that the economy is not generating enough opportunities even for the shrinking pool of job seekers.Annual PLFS data reinforce the same trend. Between 2022 and 2025, youth unemployment increased in 13 states and Union Territories, including Andhra Pradesh, Delhi, Telangana and West Bengal.The situation appears even more challenging for young women, with unemployment rising across 16 states and Union Territories during the same period.Taken together, the figures suggest that youth unemployment is becoming a structural challenge rather than a temporary fluctuation.
The problem isn't just unemployment, it's job quality
Headline unemployment figures often fail to capture the deeper challenges within India's labour market. Many graduates do find work, but not necessarily the kind of work they expected after spending years in higher education.Economist Arun Kumar said that the root of the problem is the sharp divide between India's organised and unorganised sectors."When unemployment rises, it inevitably leads to greater conflict because there are too few jobs for too many people. In India, this problem is even more pronounced because the unorganised sector employs around 94% of the workforce, while the organised sector employs only about 6%. The difference in wages and job security between these two sectors is enormous. A courier delivery worker may earn around Rs 10,000-12,000 a month, whereas a postman can earn around Rs 70,000. Naturally, nobody wants to lose an organised sector job, and everyone wants to secure one. That intense competition creates immense pressure," he added.
An analysis of India's Periodic Labour Force Survey illustrates this disconnect. Out of every 100 graduates aged between 15 and 29, only 50 are employed, 15 remain unemployed while actively searching for work, and the remaining 35 are outside the labour force altogether.Some continue their education. Others perform unpaid domestic work or have simply stopped looking for employment after repeated disappointments.Even among those who are employed, the quality of jobs remains a major concern. Only 26 out of every 100 graduates have regular salaried jobs. More strikingly, just four hold formal jobs that provide written contracts, paid leave and social security benefits.The remaining graduates are spread across self-employment, unpaid family work, casual labour and small household enterprises. Many earn irregular incomes and lack job security despite years spent pursuing higher education.The figures highlight a growing reality in India's labour market: employment alone is no longer an adequate measure of economic well-being. The challenge is increasingly about the availability of secure, productive and reasonably paid jobs.
Why educated youth feel left behind
The employment crisis begins long before students enter the labour market. Competition for limited seats in prestigious colleges has transformed education itself into an expensive investment.Government survey data show that Indian households now spend a significantly larger share of their education budgets on private coaching than they did seven years ago.The sharpest increase has been among higher secondary students preparing for engineering, medical and university entrance examinations.Families now spend nearly one-fourth of their higher secondary education budgets on coaching, compared with about 18% in 2018.Private coaching expenses have also increased steadily across primary, middle and secondary education, reflecting a growing belief that classroom teaching alone is no longer sufficient to compete in high-stakes entrance examinations.The pressure becomes particularly visible in engineering education. India had around 4.4 million undergraduate engineering students during the 2023-24 academic year. Yet the country's top 100 engineering institutions together offered only about 500,000 seats.
In effect, only one in nine engineering students can study at an institution widely regarded as offering strong placements and better career prospects.Students who fail to secure admission to elite institutions often graduate from colleges with weaker placement records, making it significantly harder to obtain well-paying jobs.The widening gap between educational aspirations and employment outcomes has created growing frustration among young people. The traditional promise that more education automatically leads to better employment is becoming increasingly uncertain.According to the State of Working India 2026 report, fewer than 7% of male graduates secure a permanent salaried job within one year of graduating. The figure is even lower, just 3.7%, when it comes to white-collar jobs.Using data from the PLFS and the earlier Employment-Unemployment Survey, the report estimates that 1.1 crore out of India's 6.3 crore graduates aged between 20 and 29 were unemployed in 2023.Graduate unemployment itself is not a new phenomenon. The report estimates that unemployment among graduates below the age of 25 increased from 35.02% in 1983 to 39.33% in 2023.What has changed, however, is the scale of the problem. India now produces far more graduates than ever before, while simultaneously entering the most important phase of its demographic transition.The country's median age currently stands at around 29 years and is expected to rise to 38 years by 2050.This is the period during which India's working-age population is expected to drive economic growth. If the economy fails to generate enough productive employment during this demographic window, the much-discussed demographic dividend could gradually turn into a demographic challenge.
India's employment paradox
India today is one of the world's fastest-growing major economies. Even amid geopolitical tensions, volatile oil prices and slowing global trade, the country has continued to post robust GDP growth and position itself as a manufacturing and investment hub.The government has invested heavily in highways, airports, railways, ports and digital infrastructure. Global technology companies such as Apple have expanded manufacturing in India, electronics exports have surged and semiconductor investments are beginning to gather pace. Policymakers increasingly see manufacturing as the sector that can absorb millions of workers and turn India's demographic advantage into sustained economic growth.Yet for many young Indians entering the labour market, this optimism feels distant. The central contradiction facing the Indian economy is that rapid economic growth has not translated into an equivalent expansion in quality employment. Economists often describe this phenomenon as "jobless growth", an economy that continues to grow without creating enough secure and productive jobs.India's challenge is especially daunting because nearly eight million graduates enter the labour market every year. Generating employment for such a large number of educated young people has become one of the country's biggest economic challenges.This gap between economic growth and employment opportunities lies at the heart of the frustration that has fuelled recent youth protests.
Is India creating enough jobs?
Whether India is creating enough jobs depends largely on which dataset is examined. The Reserve Bank of India's KLEMS database estimated that the economy generated 4.7 crore jobs during 2023-24, the highest annual increase in more than four decades.However, labour economists caution against looking at headline employment numbers alone.Employment estimates differ across official surveys because they use different methodologies. More importantly, the definition of employment itself often masks the underlying quality of jobs being created.For instance, India's labour surveys classify a person as employed if they have worked even for a few days during the reference period. Likewise, unpaid family workers and subsistence self-employed individuals are counted as employed despite earning little or no regular income.As a result, headline employment figures may paint a healthier picture than what many young workers experience in reality. Increasingly, economists argue that the more important question is no longer how many jobs India is creating, but what kind of jobs they are.
The informal sector is slowing too
For decades, India's informal economy acted as a safety valve for the labour market. Workers unable to secure formal employment often found opportunities in small businesses, family enterprises, retail trade or self-employment.However, even this safety net appears to be weakening.According to the ministry of statistics and programme implementation's latest Annual Survey of Unincorporated Sector Enterprises (ASUSE), the informal sector generated around 74.5 lakh jobs in 2025, significantly lower than the 1.1 crore jobs created during the previous survey period ending September 2024.Wage growth has also slowed sharply. Average wage growth in the sector declined to 3.9%, compared with 13% previously, suggesting that even workers who manage to find employment are seeing slower improvements in earnings.The figures reinforce concerns that employment opportunities are weakening across both formal and informal sectors, making it increasingly difficult for young people to find stable livelihoods.
India's employment quality lags behind peers
India's labour market also differs from many comparable economies because of the quality of employment available.International comparisons reveal another structural weakness: the quality of employment. Labour market studies show that around 93% of employed workers in Russia hold regular jobs. The share is about 68% in Brazil, 54% in China and 42% in Bangladesh, the PLFS 2022-23 & Jan-Mar 2024 data reported.In India, by contrast, only about 23% of workers are in regular salaried employment.This means that nearly three-fourths of Indian workers remain outside the formal sector, without written contracts, paid leave, provident fund benefits or social security.The shortage of secure employment also explains the extraordinary demand for government jobs. Whether it is railways, banking, the armed forces, civil services or state recruitment examinations, millions of candidates compete for relatively few vacancies because government employment still offers something much of the private sector cannot consistently provide stability.A government job often brings predictable salaries, pensions, housing allowances, healthcare benefits and long-term security.For many young Indians, particularly those from middle- and lower-income households, these jobs represent far more than employment. They represent financial stability for entire families.According to Kumar, the desperation is visible in the jobs educated Indians are willing to apply for.
The real issue is the lack of decent employment opportunities. We saw this clearly in Uttar Pradesh in 2017, when more than two lakh people applied for peon posts. Many applicants held qualifications such as PhDs, MTech, BTech, MCom and BCom degrees. When highly educated people apply for peon jobs, it shows they are unable to find work that matches their qualifications.
Arun Kumar
AI adds a new challenge
Even as India grapples with creating quality jobs, technological change is reshaping the employment landscape. A government-backed research group estimates that artificial intelligence could displace around three million managerial and coding jobs by the end of this decade.Automation is expected to reduce demand for routine white-collar work at a time when India is producing record numbers of engineering and technology graduates.Overseas opportunities are also becoming more limited. Tighter immigration policies in countries such as the United States, the United Kingdom and Australia have reduced opportunities for skilled Indian professionals.For decades, migration acted as a safety valve for India's educated workforce. That pathway is becoming increasingly uncertain."Many young Indians even leave the country in search of better opportunities. Some spend lakhs of rupees to migrate, while others take illegal routes because they see very few prospects at home. In many cases, they still end up doing low-paying or menial jobs abroad. That reflects the level of desperation created by the lack of opportunities in India,"Kumar noted on the brain-drain situation in India.
India's demographic dividend at a crossroads
India possesses one of the world's youngest populations, a demographic advantage that economists have long viewed as one of the country's greatest strengths.A growing working-age population has the potential to accelerate economic growth, boost productivity and expand domestic consumption.But demographic dividends are never automatic. They depend on whether an economy can generate enough productive employment for the millions entering the labour market every year.Research suggests that India's employment intensity of growth, the ability of economic expansion to generate jobs has steadily declined over the past four decades.
When NEET became the tipping point
Against this backdrop, the NEET-UG 2026 paper leak became much more than an examination controversy. Millions of students spend months and often years preparing for the country's most competitive entrance examinations.Families invest heavily in coaching classes, relocate to education hubs and, in many cases, students take gap years in pursuit of a medical seat.When allegations emerged that the examination paper had been leaked and sold before the test, the issue struck at the heart of a system that already demanded enormous financial and emotional investment.The government cancelled the examination, handed the investigation to the Central Bureau of Investigation and ordered a re-examination.For lakhs of aspirants, particularly those from middle- and lower-income households, the cancellation meant far more than repeating a test. It meant another year of uncertainty after months of preparation and considerable financial sacrifice.Some students performed worse in the re-examination. Others worried they had lost their best chance of securing admission. Reports of severe psychological stress and alleged student suicides linked to the controversy further intensified public anger.What began as protests against examination irregularities gradually evolved into a wider movement about education, unemployment and shrinking opportunities.It was in this atmosphere that the Cockroach Janta Party found resonance among young Indians. Initially known for satirical social media posts, the movement soon expanded into organised protests questioning paper leaks, unemployment, inflation and what participants described as the growing disconnect between educational aspirations and employment opportunities.The group's unusual symbol, the cockroach, captured widespread attention.The insect represented resilience, survival and invisibility, mirroring how many young people felt overlooked despite years of education and preparation. Eventually, the protests became one of the biggest youth movements witnessed in recent years.The protests exposed far more than frustration over one examination. They revealed a widening disconnect between education, employment and economic expectations.Economist Arun Kumar says unemployment extends far beyond those who are officially counted as jobless. "Youth unemployment, particularly among those aged 15 to 29, is extremely high, and the situation is especially difficult for women. There are different forms of unemployment. First, there are those actively looking for work but unable to find it. Second, there are people who are technically employed but only in low-paid, part-time or menial jobs that do not provide a decent livelihood," he said."Third, there is disguised unemployment, where people appear to be working but contribute little to productive economic activity. Finally, there are those who have stopped looking for work altogether because they have lost hope. Women are disproportionately represented in this last category. Female labour force participation in India remains much lower than in many other major economies, which means many women are no longer even counted among active job seekers," he added.Over the past few decades, India has dramatically expanded access to higher education, produced record numbers of graduates and remained one of the world's fastest-growing major economies.But the growth in quality jobs has failed to keep pace with the growing pool of educated youth. For many young Indians, securing a degree no longer guarantees a stable career or upward social mobility.
That gap between aspirations and opportunities lies at the heart of the growing frustration. For millions of students, the question is no longer just whether examinations are conducted fairly. It is whether years of education, expensive coaching, repeated attempts at competitive exams and immense financial sacrifices will eventually lead to a secure, well-paying job. Without that, the frustrations exposed by such protests are likely to persist long after the headlines fade.

Her reporting also focuses on policy, governance and economic developments, with a close lens on how decisions in corridors of power affect everyday lives and community well-being.

NEW DELHI: Even as exclusive breastfeeding rates have improved globally over the past decade, India continues to lag behind, with the proportion of infants exclusively breastfed for the first six months declining from 63.7% in NFHS-5 (2019-21) to 55.8% in NFHS-6 (2023-24).Ahead of World Breastfeeding Week (August 1-7), the World Health Organization (WHO) and UNICEF called for stronger support systems for mothers, saying global exclusive breastfeeding has increased from about 37% in 2012 to over 47% today, driven by sustained investments in health systems, community counselling and maternity protection. However, the agencies said progress remains uneven and many countries continue to fall short of global targets.Responding to a question in the Rajya Sabha, the Union health ministry attributed the decline in India's exclusive breastfeeding rate to multiple factors, including socio-cultural practices, family customs, individual preferences, the use of pre-lacteal feeds and infant milk substitutes, and breastfeeding frequency.The ministry, however, highlighted improvements in other breastfeeding indicators.
Early initiation of breastfeeding within one hour of birth increased from 41.8% to 50.1%, while the proportion of infants below six months receiving any breast milk rose marginally from 95.1% to 95.6%.The Rajya Sabha question had sought to know whether the government had assessed the impact of rising Caesarean deliveries, inadequate postnatal lactation counselling and early return to work, particularly among women in the informal sector. While the ministry did not provide findings of any such assessment, it said the National Health Mission promotes exclusive breastfeeding through the Mother Absolute Affection (MAA) programme, lactation management centres, healthcare worker training, Poshan Tracker-based counselling and community awareness campaigns.
It also cited a 2025 NITI Aayog evaluation, which found that new mothers were receiving information on exclusive breastfeeding during the postnatal period.Calling breastfeeding one of the most effective public health interventions, WHO and UNICEF said it provides essential nutrition, protects children against infections, strengthens immunity, supports cognitive development and lowers mothers' risk of breast and ovarian cancers and type 2 diabetes. The agencies said scaling up proven interventions, including skilled breastfeeding support, community counselling, paid maternity leave, supportive workplace policies and stronger regulation of breast-milk substitute marketing, could prevent nearly 400,000 child deaths and 140,000 maternal deaths globally every year.

Cong hits back after Rahul faces FIR over Parliament protest
NEW DELHI: Congress leader Pawan Khera on Sunday defended leader of opposition in the Lok Sabha Rahul Gandhi after an FIR was registered against him and other opposition MPs over a protest linked to the alleged misuse of Ram Temple donations, saying the BJP-led government was ignoring the real issue instead of addressing the allegations.His remarks came after Varanasi Police registered an FIR against Rahul Gandhi, Pappu Yadav and Awadhesh Prasad following a complaint by a group of seers over a skit staged in the Parliament complex.
Speaking to reporters, Khera said the government was focusing on filing cases against opposition leaders while overlooking allegations related to temple donations."FIRs are being filed on MPs, but the government forgets that when donations are stolen, it also hurts the sentiments of devotees," Khera said.The controversy stems from a demonstration in Parliament in which Purnia MP Pappu Yadav, dressed as a temple priest and other opposition MPs staged a symbolic performance involving a donation box while alleging corruption in Ram Temple donations.The protest prompted BJP leaders, including Bansuri Swaraj, to file complaints in Delhi, accusing the opposition leaders of hurting Hindu religious sentiments. Apart from the Varanasi FIR, another police complaint has also been filed against Pappu Yadav in Delhi.
Khera backs Rahul on delimitation
Khera also supported Rahul Gandhi's recent remarks opposing the proposed delimitation exercise, saying states likely to lose political representation should oppose the move."All those who are concerned about their states should oppose delimitation," Khera said.His remarks come amid renewed political debate over the proposed Delimitation Bill.During a recent visit to Tamil Nadu, Rahul Gandhi alleged that delimitation was an attempt to reduce the state's political influence."There is an attempt by the BJP to carry out delimitation. Delimitation is designed to disenfranchise people and take away the political power of the people of Tamil Nadu. This is a BJP conspiracy... Anyone who supports delimitation is betraying Tamil Nadu, betraying the future of Tamil Nadu, and allowing the RSS and BJP to attack the people of Tamil Nadu and its future," Rahul Gandhi had said.
Why was the FIR registered?
The FIR was lodged at Kotwali police station in Varanasi after a group of seers accused Rahul Gandhi, Pappu Yadav and Awadhesh Prasad of hurting religious sentiments through the Parliament protest.According to police, the case has been registered under multiple provisions of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS), including promoting enmity between groups, deliberate acts intended to outrage religious feelings, and offences committed with common intention.
The complaint was filed by Patalpuri Peethadhishwar Jagadguru Balak Devacharya, who alleged that the use of saffron robes and the donation-box skit insulted the Sanatan tradition and Lord Ram."Pappu Yadav wore Bhagwa and posed as a sadhu while staging a drama on the Parliament premises to portray donation theft. Rahul Gandhi and Awadhesh Prasad made gestures of putting donations into a donation box. They used Bhagwa for a political demonstration, mocked the Sanatan tradition and Lord Ram, and insulted the faith of crores of Hindus," Devacharya said.He further alleged that the performance was a coordinated attempt to mock Sanatan traditions and warned of protests if action was delayed. Police said the investigation into the case has begun.

Mayawati X post

MNS chief Raj Thackeray on Sunday launched a sharp attack on industrialists and public figures who praise Prime Minister Narendra Modi and the BJP government while choosing to live abroad, questioning their claims that India had improved significantly under the current administration. Speaking at the 20th anniversary rally of the Maharashtra Navnirman Vidyarthi Sena in Mumbai, Thackeray cited actors Vivek Oberoi and R Madhavan as examples and linked their decisions to what he described as growing frustration among the country's youth.Claiming that the government had itself acknowledged in Parliament that entrepreneurs were leaving India, Thackeray argued that many of those who publicly endorse the government's narrative were unwilling to build their own lives in the country.
"Vivek Oberoi, who played Modi's role in the movie on Modi's life, lives in Dubai. R. Madhavan, who goes on about how everything became great during Modi's time and how the country changed, moves to Dubai with his family. If you think Modi has made everything so great, then why are you settling abroad? These people will come here to work in government-sponsored films and then go back to Dubai," he said.
He added that the trend was not limited to actors, saying, "Industrialists are going abroad."Thackeray said the migration of entrepreneurs and young professionals reflected a deeper crisis of confidence, arguing that Indian cities had failed to provide the quality of life that many young people expected.
"This government made a big fuss about 'Smart Cities.' Where are those Smart Cities? Not a single city here is proper. Today, kids are going abroad. Why? Because they don't feel like living here. The cities are ruined; there's no place to take children out. Abroad, there are excellent roads, fields, gardens, cleanliness, sports complexes, everything. Because of all this, these kids feel like going abroad and settling there. And we feel nothing about it?" he said.The MNS chief also weighed in on Prime Minister Modi's remarks condemning abusive language directed at him and his mother, saying he agreed that such language was unacceptable but accused the BJP of nurturing a culture of online abuse."The language used against him was indeed inappropriate. No one should use such language about anyone. It was wrong. But tell this to your people too. Since 2012, the troll army that your party has nurtured trolls everyone, from Mahatma Gandhi, Pandit Jawaharlal Nehru, to Indira Gandhi, to all of us including me, in the filthiest ways. Today, if artists in Maharashtra take a stand against the government, they get trolled. Tell your people about all this sometime. You reap what you sow," he said.He continued, "The Prime Minister said wrong things were said about his mother. That was indeed wrong. Such things shouldn't happen. But tell your party people that others have mothers too. Tell the trolls you've nurtured. You say, 'The kids have been forgiven.' But who will apologize for what your people did? Those who ordered lathis on students, those who split students' heads open, who will they ever apologize?"Addressing student activists, Thackeray argued that recent protests should not be viewed merely through the lens of the NEET examination controversy. He said the unrest reflected wider concerns over unemployment, privatisation, poor infrastructure, corruption and the lack of opportunities."The protests that happened weren't just because of the NEET exam chaos. Go beyond that and think about what's simmering in the minds of the boys and girls, the young men and women," he said, warning that further public anger could erupt if those concerns remained unaddressed.
Quoting Osho, Thackeray rejected the suggestion that the country's youth had gone astray. "Who says the country's youth is wandering on the wrong path? If the path-makers have built the wrong path, what's the fault of the youth?" he said.He urged members of the Maharashtra Navnirman Vidyarthi Sena to understand the aspirations and anxieties of both urban and rural youth in Maharashtra, saying the movement needed to engage with the realities facing the state's younger generation.

NEW DELHI: Congress leader Rahul Gandhi on Sunday expressed deep sorrow over the devastation caused by heavy rains in Kerala, offering condolences to the families of eight people who lost their lives and urging party workers to assist in relief and recovery operations."Deeply saddened by the devastation caused by heavy rains across Kerala. My heartfelt condolences to the families of the eight people who have lost their lives. May those still missing be found safe, and the injured make a swift recovery," he said in a post on X.
The Congress leader also added that the state government was making every possible effort to support affected families and coordinate relief operations. "I urge all Congress workers and volunteers to assist these efforts in every possible way," he said, urging people to remain vigilant, especially in hilly regions, and follow authorities' guidance.
"Kerala stands united in this difficult hour. I stand firmly with every affected family," Rahul Gandhi added.Kerala chief minister V D Satheesan confirmed that eight people have died, an equal number are missing and 13 others injured in the heavy rains that triggered landslides, waterlogging and property damage across the state. In a statement, he said 27 houses were completely destroyed, 196 homes partially damaged and 5,792 people have been shifted to 209 relief camps.
Satheesan said that despite a reduction in rainfall, people should remain vigilant, especially in hilly areas. He said the government would ensure assistance to families of the deceased and those who lost homes and livelihoods.Revenue minister A P Anilkumar told reporters the situation was improving and was under control. Fishermen and fishing boats were also deployed for quick response.

Karnataka BJP chief reaches out to CM Vijay over water-sharing dispute
NEW DELHI: Karnataka BJP president BY Vijayendra has written to Tamil Nadu chief minister Vijay, urging him to adopt a cooperative approach to the long-running Cauvery water dispute and support the proposed Mekedatu reservoir project, saying the river should 'unite our people, rather than divide them.'The appeal comes amid renewed tensions between Karnataka and Tamil Nadu after the Cauvery Water Management Authority (CWMA) directed Karnataka to release 3,500 cusecs of water per day to Tamil Nadu for 15 days.
The direction has triggered protests in Karnataka, while the DMK has moved the Supreme Court seeking implementation of the water release order and clearance of the accumulated shortfall.In his letter, Vijayendra said differences between neighbouring states were natural but should be resolved through dialogue and statesmanship."As neighbouring states, differences are inevitable. What matters is how we resolve them," he wrote.
Referring to the earlier resolution of the dispute over the Thiruvalluvar statue in Bengaluru, Vijayendra said former Karnataka chief minister BS Yediyurappa and former Tamil Nadu chief minister M Karunanidhi had demonstrated that difficult issues could be settled when larger public interest prevailed."Their maturity demonstrated that even difficult issues can be resolved when the larger interests of our people prevail.
That is the spirit in which I appeal to you today," he wrote.The Karnataka BJP chief said the Cauvery was a lifeline for crores of people in Bengaluru and several towns across the Cauvery basin, including both Kannadigas and Tamilians living in Karnataka."At a time when inadequate and erratic monsoons have placed enormous stress on farmers and citizens alike, their concerns cannot be overlooked," he said.Vijayendra also urged Vijay to reconsider Karnataka's proposed Mekedatu reservoir project, saying it would help meet Bengaluru's drinking water needs without affecting Tamil Nadu's legitimate share of Cauvery waters."I also appeal to you to view the Mekedatu project in the spirit of cooperation. It can significantly address Bengaluru's drinking-water requirements without compromising the legitimate water needs of Tamil Nadu," he wrote."Your support for the project can become a powerful symbol of cooperation between our two states."He expressed hope that Vijay would take a 'statesmanlike position' that protected Karnataka's interests while respecting those of Tamil Nadu."I sincerely hope you will take a statesmanlike position that protects Karnataka's genuine interests while respecting those of Tamil Nadu, and help strengthen the historic bond between our two states. Let the Cauvery unite our people, rather than divide them," the letter said.
The Cauvery water dispute is one of India's longest-running inter-state river disputes involving Karnataka, Tamil Nadu, Kerala and Puducherry. It centres on the sharing of the Cauvery river, which is a major source of drinking water and irrigation for millions of people.The Supreme Court's 2018 judgment largely upheld the Cauvery Water Disputes Tribunal's water-sharing formula and led to the creation of the Cauvery Water Management Authority (CWMA) and the Cauvery Water Regulation Committee (CWRC) to oversee implementation.
However, disagreements frequently resurface during years of low rainfall, with Karnataka arguing it needs water for its own drinking and irrigation requirements, while Tamil Nadu insists on releases as mandated by the tribunal and the Supreme Court.The latest flashpoint is Karnataka's proposed Mekedatu reservoir project, which the state says is intended to improve Bengaluru's drinking water supply and generate hydroelectric power.Tamil Nadu has opposed the project, arguing that it could affect its allocated share of Cauvery waters and violate the existing water-sharing framework.

Karnataka CM DK Shivakumar (centre) and former CMs Siddaramaiah (left) and BS Yeddiyurappa
NEW DELHI: Karnataka chief minister DK Shivakumar on Sunday described the Mekedatu dam project, proposed by the state government on the Cauvery river, as a "permanent solution" to the long-standing dispute between Karnataka and neighbouring Tamil Nadu over the sharing of Cauvery river water."The Mekedatu project is the permanent solution. The Supreme Court has already delivered its judgment, and the central government has also given its response. Taking all that into consideration, we should move forward without wasting any more time," he said at a press conference after chairing an all-party meeting on the Cauvery water issue, which has flared up again in recent days.
The chief minister was referring to the Supreme Court's November 2025 dismissal of Tamil Nadu's objection to Karnataka's detailed project report on the Mekedatu project. In May this year, the top court also rejected Tamil Nadu's review petition challenging the earlier judgment.The Centre, meanwhile, informed Parliament in July that the Supreme Court's order does not state that Karnataka requires Tamil Nadu's consent for any new construction across the Cauvery river.Shivakumar further urged all stakeholders to move forward without wasting any more time, taking the developments into consideration.
"Taking all that into consideration, we should move forward without wasting any more time. This is not about Tamil Nadu getting more or Karnataka getting less. We should use this opportunity to bring both states to the table, hold discussions, and resolve the issue amicably. We expect everyoneâs cooperation in this effort," the Congress leader added.
The Cauvery water dispute revolves around how the river waters should be shared between the two states, particularly during years of low rainfall.The issue resurfaced amid developments concerning the Mekedatu balancing reservoir project, proposed by Karnataka. It has been a major point of friction between the two states, with Tamil Nadu traditionally opposing it on the grounds that it would affect the flow of water downstream.The latest tensions have emerged at a time when the Congress is part of the TVK-led new state government in Tamil Nadu. The party was also an ally of the DMK, the previous ruling party, but extended only external support to the government.

NEW DELHI: The Shri Ramlila Mahasangh has asked the makers of Ranbir Kapoor-starrer Ramayana to hold a special preview screening for its representatives before the film's worldwide theatrical release, warning that it will stage protests if the request is not accepted.In a letter addressed to director Nitesh Tiwari and the film's production company, Shri Ramlila Mahasangh president Arjun Kumar sought a screening of the film ahead of its Diwali 2026 release in India and overseas to ensure it does not contain scenes that could hurt Hindu sentiments.The demand comes in the backdrop of the controversy surrounding the 2023 film Adipurush, which drew criticism over its depiction of characters and settings from the Hindu epic.Recalling the earlier controversy, Kumar said members of the Sanatan community and those associated with traditional Ramlila performances had objected to several aspects of Adipurush, including "the depiction of Lanka in black instead of gold, and the portrayal of Ravana and his army in a manner that did not align with traditional beliefs.""According to information received by the Mahasangh, Ramayana may also contain certain scenes that could hurt the sentiments of Hindus living in India and abroad.

Ramayana: Part 1 is scheduled for a theatrical release during Diwali 2026, while Ramayana: Part 2 is slated to release during Diwali 2027.

Fellow opposition leaders played devotees who came forward to place donations in a collection box.In a scripted sequence, the "priest" was shown pocketing the money instead of depositing it in the box, following which a Samajwadi Party MP, playing a devotee, confronted him over the "illegal" act.The performance prompted BJP leaders, including MP Bansuri Swaraj and several MLAs, to file formal police complaints in New Delhi, accusing the opposition leaders of hurting Hindu religious sentiments. full_text:
In India, a towel draped over an office chair often became a symbol of power, associated with a govt job.
Long ago, my father told me a story about a certain âSunil ji. Nobody ever addressed him by his first name, it was always succeeded by a âjiâ, because his office chair was covered with a towel.He would often wear a safari suit & a stiff-upper lip at family weddings. The guy with a govt job, an Afsar (officer), top billing in the arranged marriage market, despite having the lowest basic pay. At one such wedding, his wife blurted out an issue they were facing. Due to some clerical mistake, the details of their salary account was not updated, and Sunil ji wasnât receiving his salary for over 2 years. They found this anomaly just last month. My family was grudgingly impressed, and hoped one of their kids turned out to be a towel-chair guy like Sunil ji.
For much of modern Indiaâs history, there wasn't enough. Jobs. College seats. Telephones. Gas cylinders. Batsmen with a good strike rate. We were short of everything. As if our nation came out of British rule like some of the TV reporters came out of the NEET protest, Gasping for breath, barely surviving the violence with almost all of the valuables stolen, but their morality, virtue and the associated pride intact.
This was India in 1947.Such was the muscle memory of the rule, that we kept presenting our Annual budget at 5 PM IST, so that our British overlords could tune-in after having their breakfast. This tradition continued till 1999, more than 50 years after independence, until the Finance minister Yashwant Sinha, changed it to 11 AM. Imagine. The trauma of British rule never went away, it showed up in our metabolic wiring, in our insulin resistance, in our early onset of diabetes. Primarily due to the British administered famines. The bodies of our ancestors rewired to store fat. When the Brits eventually went back, they left behind quite a few problematic things like bureaucracy, Pakistan & monumental scarcity.When our leaders took over, they knew our demand vastly exceeded the supply, so they had to control the access of resources. And who do you trust to do that?Another British inheritance - The Collectorate. A regiment of people specifically trained to extract from the population, to collect revenues and give it back to the overlords, for whom serving people was optional, a hobby. A lot of them were corrupt too, In contrast there was barely any corruption among British officers, because they were paid almost 70 times the Indian officers. Hence, the Indians had to compensate with corruption. As we know, they continued compensating beyond independence as well. This coterie was assigned to allocate resources to Indians.No wonder, they acquired tremendous power. People began paying to jump the queue. When the government decided who could manufacture, import or expand a factory, permissions themselves became valuable commodities. British raj was eventually succeeded by Inspector Raj. And the underpaid inspectors lived in the same bungalows the British lived in.Economist Robert Klitgaard famously summarized it as:Corruption = Monopoly + discretion - accountabilityWhenever one person has monopoly over a decision, wide discretion, and little accountability, corruption happens.Accountability was like Vitamin-D for the country. We were always deficient. Add to that a lethargic judiciary. Some even justified corruption saying it's an essential lubricant for files to move without friction. A tool to facilitate ease of doing business. Many of the Indian billionaires today, exist due to their ancestors greasing their file-folders with this lubricant generously.Corruption is a chronic illness, it has been embedded in the DNA of a drought-coded, resource starved nation like ours. A government comes to power riding a wave of public anger. The previous regime is portrayed as irredeemably corrupt. Files are opened. Committees are formed. Raids happen. People are content. Finally, someone is cleaning the system.For a while, it genuinely feels different. Time passes, Power stops feeling temporary. The government begins winning elections. The public approval remains high. Loyalists become more confident. Criticism starts sounding less like feedback and more like conspiracy. Every institution gradually fills up with people who think alike.Corruption creeps up again. Like a virus - a parasite that needs a host - like a mosquito or a bat or a pigeon.Parasites don't advertise themselves. They attach themselves to something stronger. In India's case, this host is often identity - caste, religion, language. Every political movement needs an emotional engine. That engine mobilises voters, creates loyalty and builds political capital. Most of the time these issues are legitimate and deeply important. But once emotions become intense enough, they also become excellent camouflage. People stop asking uncomfortable questions because larger battles appear to be underway.
If my religion is under threat, why discuss the waterlogged street near my house?If my caste is finally receiving justice, why focus on procurement irregularities?Not saying, Identity is not important. But we often forget to see whatâs lurking behind it. The virus keeps growing, and one day it becomes bigger than the host, voters can see it, and it gets overthrown. Exit pollsters get shamed. The power of democracy is lauded. Until a new host emerges. The cycle continues. Elections just change the wrapper of the age-old system.Corruption will go away when we make it high-risk and low-reward. High salaries & high conviction rate. A Singaporean minister earns more than a top investment banker. And their corruption watchdog has a conviction rate of 99%. Our ED has at ~1%. This is the crux, until we fix it - another Sunil ji will discover they have a salary account a decade later.

full_text:
Participants in the Jain Summer Program pose for a group photograph at Jain Vishwa Bharati in Ladnun, Rajasthan, on July 29. Photo by Aman Dhage/The American Bazaar
Nestled amid the arid plains of Rajasthan, about 230 miles west of Delhi, Ladnun is the kind of town many travelers might pass without a second glance. Its narrow streets, whitewashed temples, and unhurried pace stand in stark contrast to Indiaâs bustling metropolitan centers.This summer, however, the quiet town has become an unlikely destination for seekers of one of the worldâs oldest philosophies.For more than three centuries, Ladnun has been the spiritual home of the Terapanth order of Jainism, a reformist sect known for its disciplined monastic tradition and emphasis on nonviolence, self-restraint, and spiritual inquiry. Last month, those traditions welcomed an unusual group of visitors: nearly three dozen students, scholars, and faculty members from eight countries who are spending three weeks not merely studying Jainism, but living it.The immersive summer program, which began July 20 and concludes on Friday, is the result of a collaboration among Florida International University, California State University Long Beach, the Jain Education and Research Foundation (JERF), Jain Visva Bharati Institute, and southern California philanthropist Dr. Jasvant Modi, whose support made the initiative possible.Rather than treating Jainism as an academic subject confined to classrooms and textbooks, the organizers designed a program that allows participants to experience the philosophy through daily practice.
Each morning began with meditation. Students attended lectures on Jain philosophy, Prakrit â the ancient language of many Jain scriptures â and the foundational principles of âAhimsaâ (nonviolence), âAnekantavadaâ (the multiplicity of viewpoints), and âAparigrahaâ (non-attachment to possessions). They also interacted with monks and nuns, observed their disciplined routines, and experienced a lifestyle centered on simplicity, compassion, and mindfulness.âIt has been a very eventful week, and it has been a tremendous experience,â said Anne Vallely, a professor at the University of Ottawa and one of the foremost scholars of Jainism in the Western world.Describing the demanding schedule, she added, âWe have our lessons from 9:00 in the morning, and they go really into 10 oâclock, 11:00 at night.âThe program reflects months of planning by scholars in India and the United States.Florida International University, home to the first endowed chairs in Jain Studies in the United States, worked closely with California State University Long Beach, to develop the curriculum. The Jain Education and Research Foundation helped coordinate the academic and logistical aspects of the initiative, while Jain Visva Bharati opened its sprawling campus and monastic community to the international participants.At the heart of the effort is a broader mission: introducing Jain philosophy to a global audience at a time when its central teachings of nonviolence, environmental sustainability, restraint, and respect for diverse perspectives have taken on renewed relevance.Much of that vision has been championed by physician, entrepreneur, and philanthropist Dr. Jasvant Modi, whose years of support for Jain education and higher learning have helped establish academic programs across the United States. Modi, who has contributed tens of millions of dollars to educational and religious causes in the United States, India, and globally, provided the principal financial support for this yearâs summer school.âI was born in India in the Jain faith, and those principles of Ahimsa, compassion, and respect for all living beings have guided my entire life as a physician,â the La CaÃ±ada, California,-based physician entrepreneur told The American Bazaar. ââ After my medical career, I realized philanthropy allows me to heal on a larger scale, not just one patient at a time. I contribute to Jain education because I believe Americaâs young students must be exposed to this ancient wisdom of tolerance, non-possessiveness, and plurality, which is so undervalued today.âThe program also coincided with another milestone.This year marks the 300th anniversary of the founding of the Terapanth order, giving participants an opportunity to witness commemorative events while learning about one of Jainismâs most influential traditions. Established in the 18th century by Acharya Bhikshu, the Terapanth order is distinguished by its centralized leadership and disciplined monastic structure. Its monks and nuns travel extensively to spread Jain teachings rather than remaining in permanent monasteries.Throughout the three weeks, students discovered that learning extended far beyond formal lectures.Meals became lessons in mindful eating. Silence became a form of reflection. Conversations with monks and nuns often continued long after scheduled sessions ended. Participants learned not only the philosophical foundations of Jainism but also how those principles shape everyday decisions, from food and consumption to conflict resolution and environmental responsibility.For many students, the immersive setting transformed abstract ideas into lived experience.âIâm surrounded by scholars and Iâve gotten to meet with sadhvis and sadhus, and itâs just been lovely,â said Carol Rodriguez, one of the participants, who holds a Ph.D. in Jain Studies from the University of Florida.The Cuban-born scholar earned her bachelorâs and masterâs degrees in Jain Studies from Florida International University in Miami, where she translated portions of the Lilavatisara, a 13th-century work by Jain monk Jinaratnasuri.The international composition of the group further enriched the discussions. Participants brought diverse academic backgrounds and cultural perspectives, creating conversations that reflected Jainismâs emphasis on dialogue and multiple viewpoints rather than absolute certainty.Organizers hope the program will serve as a model for future international collaborations in religious studies, philosophy, sustainability, and peace education.Unlike traditional study abroad programs, the Ladnun initiative invites participants to become temporary members of a living spiritual community, where learning occurs as much through observation and daily practice as through formal instruction.
As the summer school concludes on July 7, participants will return to universities and communities around the world carrying more than lecture notes and academic credits. They will leave with firsthand experience of a philosophy that has quietly endured for millennia and memories of a small Rajasthan town where, for three weeks, Jainism was not simply studied, but lived.(Aman Dhage contributed to the report.)(By arrangement with The American Bazaar)

NEW DELHI: Commonwealth Games silver medallist and Assam boxer Lovlina Borgohain said she felt 'hurt' after noticing that the Northeast was missing from a map printed on napkins and displayed outside a popular Indian restaurant in Glasgow. The restaurant owners acknowledged the mistake and assured the Indian boxing contingent that it would be corrected.The incident took place when the Indian boxing team visited Mister Singh's India, The Home of Curry for a celebratory dinner after securing a record 10 medals, seven gold and three silver, at the Commonwealth Games.Lovlina noticed that the restaurant's branding showed an incomplete map of India without the Northeast. She immediately raised the issue with the management.Addressing the restaurant management during an interaction, Lovlina said the omission was upsetting."Please don't take this the wrong way. I felt a little hurt by this. In the map of India, our North East is missing. Yes, even outside, the map that's displayed has cut off the North East. As someone from the North East, that really hurts us. That's all I wanted to say.
Please keep this in mind next time. Thank you so much," she said.
Boxing Federation of India (BFI) president Ajay Singh, who was present at the restaurant, said there was no confrontation and that the issue was resolved amicably."There was no confrontation. It was an aberration and we pointed that out, me and Lovlina. They accepted their mistake and assured us that it will be corrected," Singh told PTI.
The restaurant is a popular Indian dining destination in Glasgow and has hosted several visiting sports teams and dignitaries over the years.Lovlina won a silver medal in the women's 75kg boxing event at the 2026 Commonwealth Games.The Tokyo Olympic bronze medallist lost a closely fought final to Australia's Emma-Sue Greentree by a 4-1 split decision, missing out on her first Commonwealth Games gold medal.The silver was Lovlina's maiden Commonwealth Games medal after earlier exits at Gold Coast 2018 and Birmingham 2022.India's boxing team has produced its best-ever Commonwealth Games campaign, winning a record seven gold and three silver medals. Yadavâs media convenor alleged the MP was targeted with a knife in what he described as an attempt to replicate the Atiq Ahmed incident.The incident occurred while Yadav was seated and speaking to the media. According to his media convenor, three or four men suddenly approached the MP and an altercation broke out. He alleged that one of the men first removed a slipper and hurled it before another attacker pulled out a knife."The attackers first took off a slipper and hurled it. When the knife was drawn to attack, our supporters and associates tried to restrain the assailant. I stepped forward and positioned myself between the attacker and Pappu Yadav, and I was beaten severely as a result," the convenor said.
He alleged he was beaten so badly by two or three individuals that he lost consciousness. "My associates carried me away from the spot. I have no further information," he said.A supporter of Yadav who was present said he instinctively put his hand in front of the MP as the knife was swung, causing the blade to graze his finger.
The situation descended into a melee, with people falling and piling on top of one another.
The convenor also alleged that Delhi Police personnel present did not intervene to protect Yadav and instead focused on taking the alleged attackers away. "I tried to help Pappu Yadav escape the scene. The police seemed to be shielding the goons... Not a single policeman stepped forward to help Pappu Yadav escape. When the assault was taking place, they focused solely on saving the goons and whisked them away from the scene. We don't know where they took them," he alleged."These people had come to stage a 'Prayagraj Part Two' â they came to replicate the Atiq Ahmed incident today," the convenor said, referring to the 2023 killing of gangster-turned-politician Atiq Ahmed and his brother in Prayagraj while they were in police custody.
The convenor said he had met the DCP earlier in the day and submitted a formal complaint warning that the MP was arriving and had been receiving constant threats on social media. "Despite knowing all this, they deployed only three or four police personnel here, and even they were merely protecting the goons," he alleged.He further alleged that several people had been positioned behind the media cameras before the incident. "There were people hiding behind the cameras, three or four of them. Suddenly, someone pulled out a knife, another a slipper... The MP was the target, no one else," he said.According to people present at the scene, the confrontation began after some men allegedly accused Yadav of insulting Sanatan Dharma. The men argued with him before one of them removed a slipper and attempted to throw it. Yadav's supporters then intervened, leading to a scuffle.
Yadav and his supporters have alleged the men were carrying knives and had intentions to kill him. The Delhi Police have not yet issued an official statement on the incident.Yadav himself alleged in a later statementthat the confrontation was an attempt on his life and linked it to threats against his family.âI came here because last night, they went to my childrenâs home. Now, you are trying to intimidate my children too; that wonât happen,â Yadav said. âI was with the press, and a conversation was underway. Amid that, there was an attempt to kill me.âHe alleged that some of those involved were calling for him to be killed, adding, âSome âBabaâ was saying, âBurn him alive,â while others were saying, âKill him.â If people hadnât been here, I would have been finished.âYadav also connected the confrontation to the ongoing controversy over alleged discrepancies involving offerings at the Ram Temple in Ayodhya.âI havenât said anything. I only asked Champat Rai or Giri Ji, where did the 200 kg of silver go? Where did the gold go?â he said.
On security concerns, Yadav said he had repeatedly sought protection. âThe Delhi Police is quite capable. I have been demanding security for a long time now. What crime have I committed?â he said.The confrontation comes days after Yadav was involved in a political controversy over a protest by opposition MPs concerning alleged theft of offerings made at the Ram Temple in Ayodhya. The demonstration drew criticism from seers and others, who accused the MPs of insulting Sanatan Dharma.

full_text:
India approved just one Chinese FDI proposal worth ₹1 crore, while clearing 13 applications from Hong Kong worth ₹610.42 crore in the last financial year, according to official data.
These approvals are important as investments from countries sharing a land border with India have been subject to prior government approval since April 2020 under Press Note 3 of the Department for Promotion of Industry and Internal Trade (DPIIT).
The measure was introduced to curb opportunistic takeovers and acquisitions of Indian companies during the COVID-19 pandemic.
Overall, the government has approved 63 FDI (foreign direct investment) proposals worth ₹10,292.67 crore, or $1.18 billion, during April 2025-March 2026, according to the DPIIT data.
Singapore emerged as the largest source of approved FDI proposals in value terms, with five proposals worth ₹3,259.88 crore ($382.52 million) receiving clearance.
This was followed by the UK, where five proposals worth ₹2,477.67 crore ($283 million) were approved, and Thailand, which received approval for two proposals worth ₹1,600 crore (about $180 million).
In March, the government eased Press Note 3 of April 2020. Under that, it stated that investors with non-controlling LBC (land border countries) beneficial ownership of up to 10% would be permitted under the automatic route, according to the applicable sectoral caps, entry routes, and other conditions.
However, it was clarified that the relaxed FDI norms will not apply to entities registered in China/Hong Kong or other countries sharing land borders with India.
Countries that share land borders with India are China, Bangladesh, Pakistan, Bhutan, Nepal, Myanmar, and Afghanistan.
India has never received significant investments directly from China. China ranks 23rd, accounting for only 0.32% of total FDI equity inflows into India between April 2000 and March 2026, at $2.51 billion (₹16,162.25 crore).
On the other hand, Hong Kong was at 15th position with only a 0.62% share ($4.91 billion or ₹31,220.30 crore) in the total FDI equity inflow reported during that period.
Like 2025-26, India had approved only one Chinese FDI proposal in 2024-25 also. It was valued at ₹28.71 crore ($3.44 million). In that fiscal, a total of 82 proposals were approved under the government route, involving a total investment of ₹39,758 crore ($4.72 billion).
From Hong Kong, 11 proposals worth ₹1,225.28 crore ($146.51 million) received approval in 2024-25.

full_text:
Hundreds of students continued their protest for the fifth consecutive day in Ranchi on Sunday (August 2, 2026) over alleged irregularities in the 14th JPSC examination, JSSC-CGL and other recruitment tests, demanding a CBI probe and reforms in the recruitment agencies.
The protesters, who have been holding an indefinite sit-in at a stadium since July 29, raised slogans such as 'Order CBI probe in JPSC', 'Long live Students Unity' and 'Shame on Hemant Soren'.
"Paper leaks in JPSC have happened several times. This time, OMR sheets of candidates have been leaked. Chief Minister Hemant Soren has ordered a CID probe, but we are not satisfied," JPSC aspirant Rahul Kumar Kranti said.
He alleged that previous probes into the Jharkhand Staff Selection Commission (JSSC)-CGL paper leak had not led to action and claimed that the latest investigation could also be "covered up" after a few months.
"We have completely lost faith in the ongoing CID probe. We demand a CBI probe into all recruitment examinations conducted by the JPSC and JSSC over the past seven years. We also demand the chief minister's resignation on moral grounds," Mr. Kranti said.
The protesters are demanding cancellation of the 14th JPSC Combined Preliminary Test held on April 19 and an independent probe by central agencies, including the CBI and Enforcement Directorate (ED), into alleged irregularities in recruitment examinations conducted by the JPSC and JSSC.
They are also demanding the introduction of a fifth option of "not attempted" in OMR sheets.
"The careers of thousands of students and aspirants are at stake due to corruption in both agencies. Most of us come from farmers' families. We only want fair opportunities based on merit," said Ankit Kumar from Giridih district.
Sneha, a tribal student from Ranchi, said protesters wanted strict punishment for those involved in alleged irregularities and cancellation of the 14th JPSC examination.
"I have been preparing for competitive examinations since 2023. But if an equal and fair chance is not given, how can I get a job? I urge CM Soren to listen to our demands," she said.
Archana Kumari from Palamu said the protesters would continue their agitation until the government addressed their demands and fixed accountability for the alleged irregularities.
"The State government is still in a sleeping mode. We are getting support from across the country. People from various cities are sending food items to the protest site. We are thankful to those helping us continue our protest," said Shyam Bihari Gupta, a student from Balumath in Latehar district.
Meanwhile, thousands of students held a torchlight procession in the state capital this evening.
The students, who are holding an indefinite sit-in at the Jaipal Singh Munda stadium, marched to Albert Ekka Chowk. There, they raised slogans against the JMM-led alliance government and demanded an impartial probe into the alleged irregularities in the 14th JPSC, JSCC-CGL and other state-level public recruitment tests.
They said if the state government does not address their concerns, they will march to the Jharkhand Assembly and stage a gherao in the next couple of days.
"We have been holding protests, but no government officials approached us to listen to our concerns on these issues. This clearly shows the insensitivity of this JMM-led alliance government towards the thousands of students and youths of the state," they alleged.

[SEP] After days of deliberations and lobbying, the much-awaited Cabinet expansion is likely to take place on Monday evening with the Karnataka government learnt to have informally sought time from Governor Thaawarchand Gehlot for the swearing-in of new Ministers at Lok Bhavan.
full_text:
After days of deliberations and lobbying, the much-awaited Cabinet expansion is likely to take place on Monday evening with the Karnataka government learnt to have informally sought time from Governor Thaawarchand Gehlot for the swearing-in of new Ministers at Lok Bhavan.
While the list containing names of the legislators to be sworn in is expected to reach Chief Minister D.K. Shivakumar on Monday morning from the Congress Central leadership, party sources said that many of the chosen legislators could be intimated soon after the list arrives.
Sources said that though the Central leadership had preferred Saturday for the swearing-in with the list being ready, it had been postponed for an ‘astrologically favourable day’, which happens to be Monday. “Informally, the government has sought time between 4 p.m. and 6 p.m. on Monday from the Governor,” sources said.
On Sunday, when presspersons asked Mr. Shivakumar about the absence of the Governor in Bengaluru, he said that Mr. Gehlot will be returning on Monday.
Sources said that speculation about who would be lucky to enter the Cabinet has been doing the rounds, but the leaders have been tight-lipped over the names. “The lists carried by Mr. Shivakumar and former Chief Minister Siddaramaiah are believed to have undergone changes as the party is looking to bring in a balance.”
The party is walking a tightrope with over 50 legislators aspiring to be Ministers, and its decision has to take into account regional, caste and community equations. “One of the important criteria has been the winnable factor in the next elections and their influence in their region to help other party candidates win in the 2028 elections,” sources said.
Sources said that competition is intense among Muslim legislators from Bengaluru that has turned out to be a stress point with elections to five corporations in Greater Bengaluru Authority region expected to be held shortly. “Similarly, with the KPCC president post going to B.K. Hariprasad, an OBC, demand for a higher share for Lingayats has emerged and there are many competing forces within the community. Some senior legislators are also lobbying for the post of the Speaker.”
The list has been drawn considering the post of the Chairman and the Deputy Chairman of the Legislative Council, sources added.

headline: Heavy silt inflow into the Pazhassi dam following intense rain and landslips in the catchment disrupted drinking water treatment, reducing water supply to parts of Kannur and adjoining areas on Sunday (August 2, 2026).
cluster_text: Heavy silt inflow into the Pazhassi dam following intense rain and landslips in the catchment disrupted drinking water treatment, reducing water supply to parts of Kannur and adjoining areas on Sunday (August 2, 2026). [SEP] Heavy silt inflow into the Pazhassi dam following intense rain and landslips in the catchment disrupted drinking water treatment, reducing water supply to parts of Kannur and adjoining areas on Sunday (August 2, 2026).
full_text:
Heavy silt inflow into the Pazhassi dam following intense rain and landslips in the catchment disrupted drinking water treatment, reducing water supply to parts of Kannur and adjoining areas on Sunday (August 2, 2026).
Kerala Water Authority (KWA) officials said the issue was not contamination but unusually high turbidity caused by excessive mud content in the raw water. They added that the water could be treated safely only after turbidity levels declined. At the Pazhassi water treatment plant, turbidity was measured at around 125 Nephelometric Turbidity Units (NTU), whereas efficient treatment is possible only when it falls below 50 NTU.
A senior KWA official said NTU measures the cloudiness, or turbidity, of water by indicating how suspended particles scatter light. Higher NTU values indicate muddier water, while lower values indicate clearer water. “The issue is not that the water cannot be treated. When turbidity is very high, the treatment capacity drops sharply and the filters clog quickly,” the official told The Hindu.
The official said water treatment was suspended after tests conducted on Saturday (August 1, 2026) night showed excessive turbidity. Engineers are monitoring water quality every hour, and pumping will resume once turbidity levels fall to safer limits, he added.
The Pazhassi treatment plant supplies around 30 million litres a day (MLD) of drinking water to Kannur town and surrounding areas, including Valapattanam and Chirakkal. The disruption has affected water supply in these areas.
According to KWA officials, the muddy water is the result of landslides and heavy runoff in the forested upper catchments, reportedly in Karnataka, that feed the Pazhassi dam. Continued rainfall could prolong the problem by keeping turbidity levels high.
Officials said the situation would improve if rainfall subsides and advised consumers to use stored water judiciously until normal pumping resumes. They added that the disruption was expected to ease once the raw water became clearer.

full_text:
Residents of the Scheduled Tribe settlement at Thoppilayi near Kakkanpara in Sreekandapuram municipality, Kannur, suspended their 17-day protest against a laterite quarry on Sunday (August 2, 2026) after the District Collector issued a temporary stop memo halting quarrying.
Protest committee convenor P. Bindu, who had been on a fast for nine days, and Uru Mooppan P. Aneesh, who continued the fast for three days, ended their hunger strike.
The protest committee alleged that a private individual had purchased land originally allotted to landless families for house construction under a surplus land scheme and obtained permission for laterite mining using fabricated documents. Residents of the tribal settlement said quarrying on the ecologically sensitive laterite hill posed a serious threat to around 50 Scheduled Tribe families living nearby. They also expressed concern that their cremation ground, community building, and drinking water tank, located close to the quarry site, could be endangered.
The quarry owners had resumed mining under police protection after securing a favourable order from the High Court. In response, the protest committee launched a relay hunger strike 13 days ago, with five people participating in different phases.
District Collector P. Vishnuraj issued the temporary stop memo after inquiries by the Department of Mining and Geology and other departments, following petitions submitted by the protest committee to the Collector and other authorities challenging the quarry permit.
The inquiry reportedly found that a public road lies within a 50-metre radius of the quarry, prompting the temporary suspension of mining.
Residents said attempts to start the laterite quarry had been made since 2023 but were abandoned following public opposition. After obtaining a favourable High Court order, the owners resumed quarrying, triggering protests by residents of the tribal settlement.
Earlier, P. Chandran and M. Remeshan, who had undertaken the initial phase of the hunger strike, were hospitalised after their health deteriorated. They were succeeded by P. Bindu and E. Shyamala. Ms. Shyamala was also admitted to hospital three days ago after her condition worsened, following which P. Aneesh continued the fast.
The Taliparamba Revenue Divisional Officer and the Tahsildar had earlier held discussions with the protesters and assured them that action would be taken against the quarry. On Saturday (August 3, 2026) afternoon, the Tahsildar reached the protest venue and read out the District Collector’s stop memo, after which the protest committee decided to suspend the agitation.
The protest committee said a public meeting would be held at the protest venue at 11 a.m. on Monday (August 3, 2026) to decide the future course of the agitation.

full_text:
A day before the result of the recently held by-election to Madhya Pradesh’s Datia Assembly seat, the Congress suspended former MLA Rajendra Bharti — whose disqualification necessitated the bypoll — from the party’s primary membership.
The suspension comes days after the Congress candidate for the bypoll, Ghanshyam Singh, accused Mr. Bharti of trying to sabotage his campaign and colluding with the Bharatiya Janata Party. Mr. Bharti, however, alleged that Mr. Singh had been colluding with senior BJP leader and former State Home Minister Narottam Mishra, who was denied the ticket by the ruling party.
“With the approval of the president of the All India Congress Committee (AICC), Mallikarjun Kharge Ji, Rajendra Bharti, former MLA from Datia, is hereby suspended from the primary membership of the Indian National Congress with immediate effect,” Harish Chaudhary, Congress general secretary in-charge of Madhya Pradesh, said in a statement.
Bypoll to the Datia Assembly seat was held on July 30 and the votes will be counted on August 3. The constituency recorded a voting turnout of 71.44%, as per the Election Commission.
The bypoll was necessitated following the disqualification of Mr. Bharti in April due to his conviction in a bank fraud case.
The BJP fielded debutant Ashutosh Tiwari, after snubbing former State Home Minister Narottam Mishra who represented the seat for three consecutive terms until his defeat to Mr. Bharti in the 2023 Assembly polls. The Congress fielded Mr. Singh, a member of the erstwhile Datia royal family and former MLA from neighbouring Sewda Assembly seat.
Towards the end of campaigning days in Datia, Mr. Bharti and Mr. Singh levelled allegations against each other, including about receiving funding from BJP leaders. Mr. Singh also accused Mr. Bharti of not supporting his campaign in the bypoll.
Speaking to The Hindu, Mr. Bharti’s son Ankit Bharti said, “Ghanshyam Singh has been very close to Narottam Mishra for several years and has worked against Congress candidates in the past. Even for this election he has received funding from Narottam as he is also working against BJP because he did not get the ticket. But he [Mr. Singh] has alleged that my father has received funding from the BJP to support their candidate [Mr. Tiwari].”
Mr. Bharti and Mr. Mishra have been political rivals for more than a decade with the former ending the BJP leader’s three-term tenure as Datia MLA in the 2023 election.
A leader close to Mr. Bharti also said he “had a role” in the BJP’s decision to deny Mr. Mishra the ticket.
